title: Survival Outcomes in Metastatic Colorectal Cancer Patients with BRAF Mutations Undergoing Targeted Chemotherapy: A Reconstructed Individual Patient Data Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
abstract: BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) represents an aggressive molecular subtype associated with poor prognosis and limited response to conventional chemotherapy. Although multiple targeted strategies, including anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), and BRAF-directed therapies, are used in clinical practice, their comparative effectiveness remains uncertain. We performed a reconstructed individual patient-data (IPD) meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate survival outcomes across targeted therapeutic classes in BRAF-mutant mCRC.A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane databases was conducted through July 2025 to identify RCTs reporting survival outcomes for BRAF-mutant mCRC. Kaplan-Meier curves were digitized and IPD reconstructed using established methods. A one-stage meta-analysis using Cox proportional hazards models was performed to estimate pooled overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Models were adjusted for study-level covariates and clustering, with Bonferroni correction applied for multiple comparisons.Eighteen RCTs comprising 11,931 participants were included. Pooled median OS was 22.3 months for BRAF-directed regimens, 17.1 months for VEGF-targeted therapy, and 10.1 months for EGFR-directed therapy across studies evaluating first-line therapy. Across first-line studies, BRAF inhibitor directed regimen was associated with significantly improved OS compared with EGFR inhibition (HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.31-0.60; P < 0.001) and improved PFS (HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.42-0.53; P < 0.001). VEGF inhibition also demonstrated superior OS compared with EGFR inhibition (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.38-0.81; p < 0.001). EGFR-directed regimen consistently demonstrated the poorest survival outcomes across analyses.In this reconstructed IPD meta-analysis, BRAF-directed therapies were associated with the most favourable survival outcomes, whereas EGFR directed regimen demonstrated limited clinical benefit in BRAF-mutant mCRC. These results highlight the importance of biologically aligned pathway-targeted therapy and provide comparative evidence to inform treatment selection in this aggressive molecular subtype.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers analyzed 18 clinical trials involving nearly 12,000 patients to compare how well different targeted drug treatments work for an aggressive type of colorectal cancer with BRAF mutations. They found that drugs directly targeting the BRAF mutation extended survival to about 22 months, compared to 17 months for drugs targeting blood vessel growth and only 10 months for drugs targeting growth factor receptors. These results suggest that matching the drug treatment to the specific genetic mutation in a patient's cancer may offer the best chance of survival.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers conducted a reconstructed individual patient-data meta-analysis of 18 randomized controlled trials comprising 11,931 participants to compare survival outcomes of targeted therapeutic strategies in BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer. The analysis used digitized Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models to estimate pooled overall survival and progression-free survival across BRAF-directed, VEGF-targeted, and EGFR-directed regimens in first-line therapy. BRAF-directed regimens demonstrated the most favorable outcomes with median overall survival of 22.3 months and significantly improved overall survival compared with EGFR-directed therapy (hazard ratio 0.43, 95% confidence interval 0.31–0.60) and improved progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% confidence interval 0.42–0.53). title: Vertebrobasilar Circulation Involvement in Histiocytic Neoplasms: The Coated Artery Sign.
abstract: Histiocytic neoplasms, particularly Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD), exhibit perivascular infiltration, and vertebrobasilar circulation involvement remains poorly characterized. We aimed to describe intracranial vertebrobasilar involvement.We conducted a case series nested within an observational cohort at a tertiary referral center. We identified patients from a predefined cohort of biopsy-proven histiocytic neoplasms. We included patients with ECD, Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH), or Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes disease (RDD) who demonstrated intracranial vertebrobasilar periarterial involvement, defined by MRI evidence of histiocytic infiltration encasing the vertebral and/or basilar arteries.Vertebrobasilar coated artery involvement was present in 3 patients with ECD (3/183, 1.6%), including 1 with mixed ECD-LCH, and 1 patient with RDD (1/88, 1.1%); no cases occurred in isolated LCH (0/144). Two patients with multisystemic ECD had incidental imaging findings without neurological symptoms. One patient developed a progressive brainstem syndrome due to an enlarging perivascular lesion, and 1 patient with RDD developed chronic progressive myelopathy from a cervicomedullary lesion encasing both vertebral arteries.Vertebrobasilar coated artery involvement can occur in histiocytic neoplasms, particularly ECD. Recognition of this imaging pattern may aid neurologists in diagnosis and help prevent neurological complications from compression or ischemic stroke.Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether histiocytic neoplasms, which are rare blood cell cancers, could involve major blood vessels in the brain's lower circulation. They found that a specific pattern of cancer cells coating these vessels occurred in a small percentage of patients with Erdheim-Chester disease and one patient with Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes disease, sometimes causing neurological symptoms like progressive weakness. Recognizing this imaging pattern may help doctors diagnose these conditions and prevent serious complications such as stroke.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers conducted a case series nested within an observational cohort at a tertiary referral center to characterize intracranial vertebrobasilar involvement in biopsy-proven histiocytic neoplasms, specifically examining perivascular infiltration patterns on MRI. The study identified patients with Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD), Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH), or Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes disease (RDD) who demonstrated histiocytic infiltration encasing the vertebral and/or basilar arteries, a pattern termed the coated artery sign. Vertebrobasilar coated artery involvement was present in 3 of 183 patients with ECD (1.6%), including 1 with mixed ECD-LCH, and 1 of 88 patients with RDD (1.1%), while no cases occurred among 144 patients with isolated LCH. Clinical presentations varied, with two patients showing incidental imaging findings without neurological symptoms, one patient developing a progressive brainstem syndrome from an enlarging perivascular lesion.

title: Periodontal disease, biomarkers of ADRD risk, and cognitive functioning.
abstract: Periodontitis is a hypothesized risk factor for cognitive impairment. Many prior studies lack information on biological markers of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) risk or genetic risk markers. We assessed the association between periodontitis, biological markers of ADRD risk, and cognitive test performance with robust adjustment for risk factors including high risk genotypes for ADRD.We use data from the United States High School and Beyond (HS&B:80) cohort study, a nationally representative sample of ∼26,830 people enrolled during high school in 1980 through midlife in 2021. Baseline data include information about educational contexts, opportunities, and outcomes; early life circumstances; and demographic group memberships. HS&B:80 data from 2021 include indicators of periodontal disease diagnosis history, blood biomarkers of ADRD risk, and multiple measures of cognitive functioning. We calculated false discovery rates (FDR) to account for multiple comparisons.Our analyses included 13,950 HS&B:80 panelists (mean age 58 years), among whom 15.2% reported a history of periodontal disease. Periodontal disease was associated with lower general cognitive functioning and scores on some domain-specific cognitive tasks; it was also associated with increased levels of pTau-181 and C-reactive protein. We find no evidence of heterogeneity in associations by sex, race and ethnicity, or number of apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 alleles. Only working memory attained a FDR < 10% after multiple comparisons adjustment.In this large, diverse, population-representative, community-dwelling sample, self-reported periodontal disease was cross-sectionally associated with cognitive functioning at age ∼60 and some biomarkers of ADRD risk although most associations were not significant after multiple comparisons corrections.Poor gum health has been suggested as a possible contributor to memory and thinking problems later in life, but many studies have not been able to account for important biological and genetic risk factors linked to Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. To better understand this relationship, we analyzed data from nearly 14,000 participants in a large, nationally representative U.S. study who were approaching age 60 in 2021. About 15% reported having been diagnosed with periodontal (gum) disease. People with a history of gum disease tended to perform slightly worse on measures of overall cognitive function and some specific thinking tasks. They also had modestly higher levels of blood markers associated with inflammation and increased risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. These associations were similar across men and women, racial and ethnic groups, and people with different levels of genetic risk based on apolipoprotein E (APOE) status. While this study cannot determine whether gum disease causes cognitive decline, the findings suggest that poor periodontal health may be potentially linked to both cognitive performance and biological signs associated with dementia risk in midlife, highlighting the importance of future research that can better understand if these observations are causal or coincidental.© 2026 The Author(s). title: Sudden Cardiac Death in Firefighters From the United States: A 16-Year Postmortem Analysis.
abstract: Sudden cardiac death (SCD) is the leading cause of duty-related death among firefighters. Understanding postmortem cardiovascular abnormalities associated with SCD is critical to guiding fire service cardiovascular disease screening and prevention programs.This study included US firefighters who had a duty-related death over a 16-year period (1999-2014) with available postmortem reports (autopsy/medical examiner reports). Cases were systematically reviewed to identify cases of SCD. For each SCD case, the primary etiology of SCD was adjudicated by experts in sports cardiology and cardiovascular pathology.Postmortem evaluations were available for 794 of 2100 (37.8%) on-duty firefighter deaths over the study period (average age, 44±13 years; age range, 17-82 years; 4.0% women). A total of 312 of 794 (39.3%) firefighter deaths were adjudicated as SCD. A total of 255 of 312 (81.8%) SCD events were attributable to coronary artery disease/ischemic heart disease or hypertensive heart disease, which both are associated with traditional cardiovascular risk factors. The leading etiology of SCD among young firefighters (aged <40 years) was also coronary artery disease/ischemic heart disease (24/50 [48.0%]). Of firefighters who had an exertional SCD event thought to be secondary to coronary artery disease (n=97), a total of 62 of 91 (68.1%) had severe fixed coronary stenosis, while 29 of 91 (31.9%) demonstrated acute plaque rupture/thrombosis.More than 80% of on-duty SCD events among US firefighters are due to coronary artery disease and hypertensive heart disease that may be prevented by early disease identification and risk factor modification. Future studies should assess the efficacy of more rigorous firefighter cardiovascular disease screening and management practices.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Obese Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction.
abstract: To evaluate whether GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), compared with DPP4 (dipeptidyl peptidase-4) inhibitors or sulfonylureas, are associated with reduced all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalizations in patients with obesity and type 2 diabetes, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.PRAISE-HFpEF (Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist in Obese Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction) was a nationwide multicenter cohort study using a new-user, active-comparator design within the national Veterans Affairs Health System (170 US hospitals). Adults with type 2 diabetes between January 1, 2000 and December 31, 2021, were identified from centralized electronic health records. Patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and a body mass index ≥30 kg/m2 were selected using a validated diagnostic algorithm. Exposure was initiation of a GLP-1RA versus DPP4 inhibitors/sulfonylurea from January 1, 2015 to December 31, 2021. The primary outcome was time to all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalization. Inverse probability of treatment weighting based on the propensity score was used to balanced baseline characteristics.Among 179 288 patients with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, 1024 GLP-1RA users and 796 DPP4 inhibitors/sulfonylurea users met inclusion criteria. Over a median follow-up of 1.5 years, GLP-1RA use was associated with a lower risk of the primary outcome (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.78 [95% CI, 0.64-0.95], P=0.01). Weight loss was modestly greater with GLP-1RAs compared with DPP4 inhibitors/sulfonylurea (-12.9% versus -10.1%).Among patients with obese heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and type 2 diabetes, GLP-1RA initiation was associated with a lower incidence of death or heart failure hospitalization compared with alternative oral agents.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a diabetes medication called GLP-1 receptor agonists could reduce death and heart failure hospitalizations in obese patients with heart failure and type 2 diabetes, comparing it to two other diabetes drugs. Among over 1,800 patients studied, those taking GLP-1 receptor agonists had a lower risk of death or hospitalization compared with the other medications, and also experienced greater weight loss. However, this was an observational study tracking existing patients rather than a controlled experiment, so it cannot definitively prove the medication caused the improvement.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Analog-Type Amyloidosis: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.
abstract: Amyloidosis is a heterogeneous group of diseases characterized by extracellular deposition of insoluble proteins. Glucagon-like peptide-1 analog (AGLP1)-type amyloidosis is a rare iatrogenic form of amyloidosis localized to areas of glucagon-like peptide-1 analog injections. In this study, we describe a case of AGLP1-type amyloidosis presenting as a subcutaneous mass on the abdomen of a 71-year-old woman with a history of liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide use. Biopsy, including Congo red stain, was consistent with an amyloid deposit. Amyloid protein identification by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry showed a typical amyloid profile with low spectra for liraglutide. Immunohistochemistry, subsequently performed, showed that the amyloid deposits were positive for glucagon; there is an extensive peptide homology between liraglutide and glucagon. Only 3 cases of AGLP1-type amyloidosis have been previously reported. It is vital for clinicians and pathologists to be aware of AGLP1-type amyloidosis given the increasing worldwide use of GLP-1 agonists, as well as the potential for misdiagnosis of systemic amyloidosis, which has profound therapeutic and prognostic implications.Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. llm_summary: Researchers documented a case of a rare side effect called glucagon-like peptide-1 analog-type amyloidosis, where abnormal protein deposits formed at injection sites in a 71-year-old woman using diabetes and weight-loss medications including liraglutide and semaglutide. Testing confirmed the deposits contained amyloid protein similar to glucagon, a natural hormone that shares structural similarities with these medications. As these injectable drugs become increasingly popular worldwide, doctors and laboratory specialists need to recognize this condition to avoid misdiagnosing it as a more serious systemic disease.
llm_summary_expert: This case report describes a 71-year-old woman who presented with a subcutaneous abdominal mass and had a history of glucagon-like peptide-1 analog use including liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide. Skin biopsy with Congo red staining confirmed amyloid deposition, and liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry identified a typical amyloid profile with low spectral signal for liraglutide. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated that the amyloid deposits were positive for glucagon, reflecting extensive peptide homology between liraglutide and glucagon. Only three cases of glucagon-like peptide-1 analog-type amyloidosis have been previously reported in the literature. Given the increasing worldwide use of GLP-1 agonists, clinicians and pathologists should be aware of this rare iatrogenic form of amyloidosis to avoid misdiagnosis of systemic amyloidosis, which carries significant therapeutic and prognostic implications.

title: Systemic Hypertension and Survival in Pulmonary Hypertension.
abstract: Pulmonary hypertension (PH), a progressive and life-threatening condition with rising prevalence among older adults, frequently coexists with systemic hypertension, the prognostic impact of which is poorly understood.To evaluate the association between systemic hypertension and survival in patients with PH.This multicenter cohort study analyzed data from the Pulmonary Vascular Research Institute GoDeep meta-registry, integrating global retrospective and prospective PH cohorts (n = 3238 in Europe, n = 3014 in North America, n = 96 in Africa, n = 802 in Asia, and n = 851 in Oceania). Survival was assessed using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models and adjusted for key confounders, with sensitivity analyses to validate robustness. Independent external validation was performed in a cohort in the UK. A total of 12 771 patients with incident PH (median [IQR] age, 65 [53-73] years; 7372 [58%] female) were diagnosed via right heart catheterization and comprehensive clinical data, encompassing PH groups 1-5 and all age categories. The study spans diagnosis decades from 1980 to 2020. Data were analyzed from February 2025 until September 2026.Center-reported diagnosis of systemic hypertension, baseline systolic systemic arterial pressure (sSAP), and heart rate as well as longitudinal sSAP and heart rate trajectories.All-cause mortality, adjusted for confounding variables, including age, PH group, antihypertensive and PH-specific medications, and cardiac index.Higher baseline sSAP and preexisting systemic hypertension were independently associated with improved survival. Patients with hypertension exhibited a 26% reduced mortality hazard (hazard ratio [HR], 0.74; 95% CI, 0.68-0.79) compared to their counterparts without hypertension. Survival benefits correlated positively with increasing sSAP (80-180 mm Hg), remained consistent across PH groups and age groups, and were independent of antihypertensive and PH-specific medications. Elevated heart rate was associated with higher mortality. sSAP increments correlated with improved cardiac index and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion. Decreased sSAP and higher heart rate during follow-up correlated with higher mortality. External validation in a separate UK cohort confirmed these findings.In this global PH cohort, higher sSAP was associated with enhanced survival, while a higher baseline heart rate and declining systemic blood pressure during follow-up were significantly associated with increased mortality risk.

title: Very short flow diverters for intracranial aneurysms: technical feasibility, angiographic outcomes, and clinical safety across diverse cerebrovascular locations.
abstract: Longer flow diverters (FDs) are often selected to facilitate deployment. Very short FDs (VSFDs; 10-12 mm) offer a targeted alternative, but technical complexity has limited their adoption, resulting in scarce clinical data.This single-center, retrospective cohort study included patients with intracranial aneurysms who underwent VSFD treatment. The primary outcome was technical success, defined as deployment of the intended VSFD across the aneurysm neck with complete neck coverage at the end of the index procedure, and analyzed per index aneurysm. Secondary outcomes included angiographic results, assessed using the O'Kelly-Marotta (OKM) grading scale, and clinical outcomes, evaluated with the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) during follow-up. Statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.5.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).Seventy-five patients harboring 151 aneurysms were included, with 86 index aneurysms treated using 93 VSFDs. title: Facial artery morphology assessed by computed tomography angiography: a mixed-effects morphometric analysis of age, sex, and laterality.
abstract: The facial artery is the principal arterial supply to the midface and is among the most frequently encountered vascular structures during facial reconstructive, aesthetic, and minimally invasive procedures. Precise knowledge of its anatomical course and morphometric characteristics is essential to minimize vascular complications. However, previous morphometric studies have largely been descriptive and have rarely accounted for bilateral anatomical correlation or simultaneously evaluated the independent effects of age, sex, and laterality using appropriate multivariable statistical models.A retrospective cross-sectional study was performed using computed tomography angiography (CTA) examinations from 103 adults, yielding 201 evaluable facial arteries. Standardized three-dimensional morphometric measurements were obtained at the inferior border of the mandible and the lateral alar base. Linear mixed-effects models incorporating patient-specific random intercepts were used to evaluate the effects of age, sex, side, and CTA diagnostic category while accounting for within-subject correlation. Measurement reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Bland-Altman analysis, and Cohen's kappa.Type III, according to the Furukawa classification, was the predominant anatomical pattern (67.2%). Among 98 patients with bilateral visualization, Furukawa type showed complete right-left concordance (100%; κ = 1.00). In an additional patient-level logistic model, neither age (OR 0.992 per year; 95% CI, 0.965-1.020; P = 0.584) nor female sex (OR 1.793; 95% CI, 0.767-4.191; P = 0.178) was significantly associated with Type III versus Type II. For continuous morphometric variables, no systematic laterality effect was detected, although individual-level bilateral agreement varied across parameters. After Holm correction across morphometric outcomes, women had a smaller facial artery diameter at the inferior border of the mandible and a shorter zygomatic arch-facial artery distance than men, while increasing age was independently associated with a shorter oral commissure-facial artery distance. Quantitative morphometric measurements demonstrated good-to-excellent observer reproducibility (intraobserver ICC: 0.900-0.960; interobserver ICC: 0.760-0.860), whereas categorical assessment of facial artery position relative to the nasolabial sulcus showed perfect intraobserver (κ = 1.00) and substantial interobserver agreement (κ = 0.79).CTA provides a reproducible morphometric assessment of the facial artery. No systematic laterality effect was identified for continuous morphometric variables, although individual bilateral agreement varied by measurement, while Furukawa type showed complete bilateral concordance in patients with both arteries visualized. Age and sex were not significantly associated with Furukawa Type III versus Type II, but they influenced selected continuous morphometric parameters. These findings characterize facial artery anatomy in a Mexican clinical cohort and may inform individualized anatomical assessment and preprocedural planning; they do not establish procedural risk thresholds.© 2026. title: Control of Diaphragm Muscle in Health and Disease.
abstract: Unique to mammals, the diaphragm muscle (DIAm) is the major pump muscle for breathing. The DIAm is a skeletal muscle composed of different fiber types with different mechanical and fatigue properties. Neural control of the DIAm is mediated by recruitment of motor units (MUs), each comprising a phrenic motor neuron in the cervical spinal cord and the set of muscle fibers (of a single type) it innervates. Thus, by recruiting different MU types, a range of motor behaviors can be accomplished. To support breathing, which is a sustained behavior, fatigue-resistant slow (type I fibers) and fast (type IIa fibers) MUs are recruited. However, the DIAm also subserves short duration, higher-force airway clearance, and voiding behaviors that require recruitment of more fatigable fast (type IIx/IIb) fibers. Importantly, in disease conditions, these fatigable DIAm MUs are more vulnerable, while fatigue-resistant MUs are more resilient.

llm_summary: The diaphragm, the main breathing muscle in mammals, contains different types of muscle fibers that are controlled by nerve cells in the spinal cord, allowing the body to perform both sustained breathing and short, forceful actions like coughing. Fatigue-resistant muscle fibers support regular breathing, while more easily fatigued fibers enable powerful but brief movements. In disease, the easily fatigued fibers become more vulnerable to damage while the fatigue-resistant fibers remain more stable.
llm_summary_expert: The diaphragm is a unique mammalian skeletal muscle that serves as the primary pump for breathing and is composed of different fiber types with distinct mechanical and fatigue properties. Neural control of the diaphragm occurs through recruitment of motor units, each consisting of a phrenic motor neuron in the cervical spinal cord and the muscle fibers it innervates, allowing for varied motor behaviors depending on which motor unit types are activated. During sustained breathing, fatigue-resistant slow type I fibers and fast type IIa fibers are recruited, whereas short-duration, higher-force behaviors such as airway clearance and voiding require recruitment of more fatigable fast type IIx/IIb fibers. In disease conditions, the fatigable diaphragm motor units demonstrate greater vulnerability compared to fatigue-resistant motor units, which show greater resilience. The differential vulnerability of motor unit types in disease suggests that understanding diaphragm motor control mechanisms is essential for comprehending how respiratory and non-respiratory functions are compromised in pathological states.

title: Comparative survival and time toxicity outcomes of CAR-T versus bispecific antibody therapies in relapsed/refractory FL.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) and CD20xCD3 bispecific antibody (BsAb) therapies are both effective for relapsed/refractory (R/R) follicular lymphoma (FL), but comparative real-world survival outcomes and time toxicity have not been characterized. We performed a multicenter retrospective study of 228 patients with R/R FL treated with standard-of-care CAR-T (n = 141) or BsAb (n = 87) across 17 U.S. academic centers in the third-line or later setting. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were stratified by 2 or ≥3 prior lines of therapy (LOT2 or LOT3+), including propensity matching. Time toxicity was measured by physical health care contact days. Median PFS was not reached (NR) with CAR-T and 581 days with BsAb in the LOT2 cohort (p < .0001), and was NR with CAR-T and 584 days with BsAb in the LOT3+ cohort (p = .0064). CAR-T recipients were younger (p < .0001) and had better performance status (p = .007) but were more refractory to prior LOT (p = .017). PFS advantages of CAR-T were independent of these differences. OS did not differ between treatment groups. CAR-T had significantly greater time toxicity over the first year, with higher mean contact days than BsAb in both the LOT2 (58 vs 44) and LOT3+ (69 vs 49) cohorts. In this large multicenter cohort of patients with R/R FL, CAR-T was associated with superior PFS but greater time toxicity compared with BsAb therapy. title: Towards modeling the hemodynamic impact of mitral and aortic valve repair in patients with left ventricular assist devices.
abstract: Valve dysfunction is a major threat to long-term success in left ventricular assist device (LVAD) therapy, with direct implications for right heart performance. In this study, we apply a patient-specific, image-based computational modeling framework to evaluate the hemodynamic impact of simulated mitral and aortic valve repair in five LVAD-supported patients. Each patient was modeled under four conditions: (patient-specific LVAD-supported state), simulated mitral valve (MV) repair, simulated aortic valve (AV) repair, and simulated combined MV&AV repair. Because validation data for valve repair were unavailable, the simulated repair scenarios are exploratory in silico interventions based on clinically validated patient-specific models. The models integrate dynamic CT imaging, echocardiography, catheterization data, and device-specific LVAD parameters into a coupled 3D-0D simulation pipeline. Valve dynamics are governed by transvalvular pressure and flow, allowing physiological modeling of regurgitant lesions and surgical repair. The right ventricular (RV) was assessed using a combination of model-derived metrics, including right ventricular ejection fraction (RVEF), pulmonary artery pulsatility index (PAPi), and RV-PA coupling. In addition, we performed blood residence time (RT) analysis to evaluate blood stasis within the left heart and aorta. The simulations suggest that valve repair improved cardiac output, reduced pulmonary congestion, and enhanced right ventricular loading conditions. Notably, mitral valve repair restored aortic valve opening during the cardiac cycle, which improved sinus washout and reduced blood residence time within the aortic root-factors associated with lower thrombotic risk. Overall, these findings suggest a potential role for valve repair in LVAD-supported hearts, though larger, validated patient cohorts are needed to confirm these results.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). title: Surveillance of C. auris and Other Potentially Pathogenic Yeast Among Anesthesia Workspace Reservoirs, Multicenter Study.
abstract: The emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) Candida auris has raised concern about fungal healthcare-associated infections in perioperative and critical care settings. We evaluated anesthesia workspaces to identify high-risk reservoirs and inform optimization of infection prevention practices.We conducted a prospective multicenter observational study of patients across 11 geographically dispersed U.S. hospitals from March 2023 to July 2025. A total of 6,074 reservoirs were sampled during 605 surgical cases and 273 consecutive operating room case pairs to detect C. auris and other potentially pathogenic yeast, including C. pseudohaemulonii, C. vulturna, C. diddensiae, C. metapsilosis, and Naganishia diffluens.No anesthesia workspace reservoirs tested positive for C. auris (95% CI 0%-0.61% for surgical cases and 0-1.34% for case pairs). Other potentially pathogenic yeast (24 isolates) were detected in 1.16% (7/605) of cases. Most isolates were recovered from patient skin (92%), with fewer from environmental surfaces (4%) and practitioner hands (4%). Potential transmission patterns reflected known C. auris epidemiology, including patient-to-environment and patient-to-patient spread.Outside outbreak settings, the anesthesia workspace for the studied population appears to be a low-risk reservoir for C. auris, making routine empirical environmental interventions such as high-dose ultraviolet-C irradiation difficult to justify. Surveillance for other potentially pathogenic yeast may provide a more practical approach to guide targeted infection prevention efforts.Copyright © 2026 Association for Professionals in Infection Control and Epidemiology, Inc. title: Event-to-Payment Latency in Physicians With Imaging-Related Allegations: NPDB Reports Processed 2004-2025.
abstract: To characterize event-to-payment/report-processing latency among physicians with imaging-related allegations.This retrospective cross-sectional study included National Practitioner Data Bank physician payment reports processed in 2004-2025, excluding state-fund reports. Imaging-related allegations were identified in either specific-allegation field. Latency equaled original report-processing year minus alleged-event end year, using onset year when end year was unavailable. Adjusted models included report characteristics and jurisdiction, with practitioner-clustered standard errors. Complementary analyses examined events in 2004-2010 and jurisdiction random effects.Among 199,060 eligible reports, 1,980 involved imaging-related allegations (1,852 physicians). Median latency was 4 years (IQR, 3-6); 47.0% had latency ≥5 years. The proportions were 43.7% (2004-2009), 42.9% (2010-2015), 46.1% (2016-2020), and 55.7% (2021-2025). Adjusted differences were +0.66 years for permanent injury and +0.48 for death versus nonpermanent injury; +0.38 for outpatient and +0.49 for mixed settings versus inpatient care; and +1.56 for judgment versus settlement/other. All corresponding 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. Age was associated with -0.16 years per decade-category increment. Among 562 reports for events in 2004-2010, median latency was 4 years and 44.1% had latency ≥5 years. The adjusted payment ratio per additional latency year was 1.021 (95% CI, 0.997-1.044; P=0.082).Paid reports involving physicians with imaging-related allegations frequently reflected care delivered years earlier. The payment association was small, imprecise, and not statistically significant. title: Bayesian methods in nephrology: applications in adaptive trials, dynamic risk prediction, pharmacokinetics, and causal inference.
abstract: Bayesian statistics is gaining momentum in biomedical research, offering a flexible and intuitive framework for integrating prior knowledge, managing uncertainty, and informing decision-making. In nephrology, a field marked by complex pathophysiology, small patient populations, and evolving therapeutic landscapes, Bayesian approaches may provide critical advantages over traditional statistical methods. Bayesian methodologies may help reshape nephrology by improving trial efficiency, refining diagnostic and prognostic precision, and strengthening causal inference. We conducted a comprehensive narrative review of peer-reviewed literature on Bayesian applications in nephrology, highlighting studies in adaptive clinical trial designs, dynamic risk prediction models, network meta-analyses, pharmacokinetic modeling, and Bayesian Mendelian randomization approaches, including Bayesian model averaging frameworks. Bayesian adaptive designs enabled more efficient and ethically sound trials, such as the WIndow-of-opportunity clinical trial platform for evaluation of novel treatment strategies in REnal cell cancer (WIRE) platform study in renal cell carcinoma. In diagnostics and prognostics, Bayesian models allowed individualized inference from dynamic data, as demonstrated in estimated glomerular filtration rate trajectory analyses and mortality prediction. Bayesian network meta-analyses improved comparative effectiveness research by incorporating probabilistic treatment rankings, while Bayesian frameworks strengthened causal inference through methods like Mendelian randomization (MR) -Bayesian Model Averaging and Bayesian Kernel Machine Regression. Bayesian approaches have emerging applications in nephrology, promoting a probabilistic framework that enhances the interpretation of complex clinical and research data and supports more individualized patient care. Their integration into both research and clinical practice requires investment in education and training, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the development of accessible analytical tools. Embracing Bayesian methods is likely to play an important role in advancing precision medicine and improving patient outcomes in nephrology.© The Author(s) 2026. Bayesian adaptive trial designs demonstrated improved efficiency and ethical soundness, exemplified by the WIRE platform study in renal cell carcinoma, while Bayesian models enabled individualized inference from dynamic clinical data such as estimated glomerular filtration rate trajectories and mortality predictions. Bayesian network meta-analyses enhanced comparative effectiveness research through probabilistic treatment rankings, and Bayesian frameworks strengthened causal inference through methods including Mendelian Randomization-Bayesian Model Averaging and Bayesian Kernel Machine Regression. The authors identified that Bayesian approaches offer critical advantages in nephrology by integrating prior knowledge, managing uncertainty in small patient populations, and supporting more individualized patient care through probabilistic interpretation of complex clinical data. Successful implementation of Bayesian methods in nephrology requires substantial investment in education and training, interdisciplinary collaboration, and development of accessible analytical tools to advance precision medicine in the field.

title: An overlooked Ally: Confronting the rehabilitation gap in modern cellular therapies-A scoping review with narrative synthesis of publicly available cellular therapy conference programs.
abstract: Despite growing evidence supporting the benefits of rehabilitation across the treatment continuum, the extent to which physiotherapy (PT) is represented at professional hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) and chimeric antigen receptor therapy (CAR-T) conferences remains unclear. This study therefore aimed to evaluate the visibility of PT content at major international HCT and CAR-T conferences over the past 5 years.A scoping review of publicly available conference programs and proceedings was conducted for major HCT and CAR-T conferences held between 2021 and 2025 across Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the Middle East (n = 28 conferences). Programs were screened for PT-related content presented as dedicated sessions or within multidisciplinary, supportive care, nursing, or survivorship programs. For contextual comparison, oncology PT conferences (n = 4) held during the same period were also reviewed.Dedicated PT or rehabilitation scientific tracks were uncommon across the HCT and CAR-T conferences reviewed. PT/rehabilitation related content, where identified, was typically embedded within broader nursing, supportive care, or survivorship sessions. The International Society of Pediatric Oncology demonstrated the most consistent inclusion of rehabilitation-related presentations, while limited abstracts were identified within selected HCT conferences despite the absence of dedicated PT tracks. In contrast, oncology PT conferences consistently included dedicated rehabilitation-focused scientific sessions.This review identified limited visibility of PT and rehabilitation within publicly available HCT and CAR-T conference programs despite the growing evidence supporting rehabilitation across the cellular therapy continuum. These findings highlight an opportunity to strengthen multidisciplinary engagement and improve the visibility of rehabilitation science within future conference programs. However, conference programs represent only one component of knowledge translation and cannot determine whether observed representation reflects abstract submission patterns, conference programming decisions, or the broader rehabilitation research landscape. Future studies evaluating abstract submission and acceptance data are warranted.Copyright © 2026 Hematology/Oncology and Stem Cell Therapy.

title: When In-Person Interpretation Matters: Perspectives From ICUs and Acute Inpatient Care Settings.
abstract: Clinicians often care for multilingual patients and generally prefer in-person rather than remote interpretation. However, little is known about the reasons for selecting specific interpretation modalities in intensive care units (ICUs) and acute inpatient care settings.To examine the context and application of in-person interpretation in ICUs and acute care settings.Semistructured interviews of interprofessional stakeholders were conducted to understand the advantages and limitations of in-person and remote interpretation modalities in ICUs and acute care settings. Thematic analysis of the interviews was performed.Forty-one interviews were completed. Certain contexts motivated preferences for selecting in-person rather than remote interpretation in ICUs and acute care settings. Three overarching themes were identified: (1) specific types of conversations (eg, goals-of-care, end-of-life, and difficult conversations), (2) additional patient-related communication barriers (eg, hearing problems, delirium), and (3) other considerations related to in-person interpreter expertise (cultural contexts and prebriefing) and barriers to use (eg, delays, difficulty contacting interpreters).Acute care clinicians often prefer in-person interpretation owing to factors that are either specific to in-person interpretation or cannot be fully replicated via remote modalities. Acute care clinicians consider conversation complexity, patient factors, and unique benefits versus logistical barriers when considering in-person interpretation. Overall, in-person interpretation provides advantages over alternative modalities for several scenarios to improve the quality of care for patients with non-English language preference in ICUs and acute care settings.©2026 American Association of Critical-Care Nurses.

title: Laryngeal Injuries Following General Endotracheal Anesthesia: A Case Series.
abstract: Endotracheal intubation can cause laryngeal injury, with clinical presentation ranging from transient hoarseness to persistent vocal cord immobility. This study examines the incidence, clinical features, and outcomes of post-intubation laryngeal injuries following procedures traditionally considered low risk for such complications.We conducted a retrospective review of adult patients who underwent tracheal intubation for surgical procedures between May 1, 2018, and December 31, 2024, and subsequently presented with postoperative laryngeal injury-related symptoms. Patients who underwent cardiothoracic, thyroid, parathyroid, or anterior cervical spine procedures were excluded. We reviewed patient demographics, airway and intubation characteristics, treatments, and clinical outcomes.Among 267 824 patients undergoing 454 924 general anesthetics, 30 developed postoperative laryngeal injury (6.6/100 000; 95% CI 4.5-9.4) which did not resolve spontaneously and required laryngology evaluation. Of these 22 (67%) had well defined movement abnormalities: unilateral (n = 15) and bilateral vocal cord immobility (n = 1), unilateral hypomobility (n = 4), bilateral hypomobility (n = 1), combined unilateral vocal cord immobility with contralateral hypomobility (n = 1), and 11 (33%) had no movement abnormality. Twenty-one (64%) were intubated via video laryngoscopy. Follow-up was available for 21 patients (70%) with a median [IQR] duration of 12 [9-35] months; 15 (72%) showed partial improvement without complete resolution, while 6 showed no improvement.Laryngeal injury following general anesthesia with tracheal intubation is a uncommon complication. In our series, approximately two-thirds of patients had identifiable injuries, while one-third exhibited no structural abnormality. While 75% of patients demonstrated partial symptomatic improvement, however, complete resolution was not observed in any of the patients who received follow-up in our institution, underscoring the severity of this complication.

title: Bile Acid Malabsorption Panel in Patients with Treated Neuroendocrine Tumors.
abstract: Patients with neuroendocrine tumors experience diarrhea due to bioactive products of neuroendocrine tumors, bile acid malabsorption, or small bowel resection. We previously validated a bile acid malabsorption panel based on single stool primary bile acid (> 10%) and fasting serum C4 (> 52.5 ng/mL) to diagnose bile acid malabsorption.Our aim in this study was to audit diagnosis of bile acid malabsorption using the bile acid malabsorption panel in patients with treated neuroendocrine tumors compared with patients with functional diarrhea.Bile acid malabsorption was identified in 14/23 (61%) patients with neuroendocrine tumors based on combined C4 and single stool primary bile acid. Bile acid malabsorption was more prevalent in patients with NET than in patients with functional diarrhea as demonstrated by significantly higher primary bile acids and serum C4.The bile acid malabsorption panel is a feasible convenient test to positively diagnose bile acid malabsorption in patients with neuroendocrine tumors.© 2026. title: How Would We Treat Our Own Weaning From Microaxial Flow Pumps for Left Ventricular Unloading?
abstract: A personalized rather than "one-size-fits-all" approach is essential when weaning patients from microaxial flow pumps (Impella). We detail, for the first time, a structured, stepwise, multimodal, bedside strategy to guide safe and effective discontinuation from a microaxial flow pump, based on echocardiography, reconditioning, and use of inotropes, Impella support, stepwise reduction titrated according to hemodynamics, and lung ultrasound with VExUS when appropriate ("E.R.I.L." protocol). Integrating these 4 pillars into daily clinical practice, E.R.I.L. aims to identify the optimal timing for discontinuation of microaxial flow pump use, whether used as isolated mechanical circulatory support or combined with V-A ECMO (ECPELLA), thereby minimizing device-related complications while preserving the duration of support needed to achieve sustained left ventricular recovery.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. title: Unintentional Weight Loss Does Not Predict Poor Outcomes in Zenker Diverticulum.
abstract: Weight loss is frequently considered a cardinal presenting symptom for patients with Zenker diverticulum (ZD). We hypothesized that weight loss in patients with cricopharyngeal muscle dysfunction (CPMD), with or without diverticula, was associated with the length of symptoms and size of diverticulum.Prospective, multicenter observational study of CPMD patients with and without diverticula reporting unintentional weight loss (+WL) or no weight loss (-WL) prior to enrollment in the Prospective Outcomes of Cricopharyngeal Hypertonicity (POuCH) database. abstract: Despite the continued absence of a definitive biomarker for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), research over the last three decades has identified a wide range of underlying pathophysiological abnormalities. Peripheral mechanisms include gastrointestinal infection, changes in the gut microbiome, visceral hypersensitivity, increased intestinal permeability, low-grade mucosal inflammation and altered immune function, abnormal gastrointestinal motility, and the role of serotonin, bile acid metabolism, and carbohydrate metabolism. Central mechanisms include psychological health and altered central pain processing. These central and peripheral mechanisms can act in an integrated way to cause IBS symptoms, via the gut-brain axis, supporting the concept of IBS as a disorder of gut-brain interaction. Some mechanisms can be quantified using validated tests and questionnaires, including abnormal bile acid metabolism, accelerated colonic transit, and psychological comorbidity. However, more work is needed to translate most mechanisms into reliable tests able to identify specific targets for treatment. This Review discusses the current understanding of the pathophysiology of IBS in terms of peripheral, central, and integrated mechanisms.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: The role of Vagus nerve stimulation in epilepsy with eyelid myoclonia - A case series.
abstract: To study the effectiveness of vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) in patients with epilepsy with eyelid myoclonia (EEM, previously known as Jeavons Syndrome).EEM is an epilepsy syndrome characterized by eyelid myoclonia, eyelid closure-induced generalized EEG paroxysms or seizures, and photosensitivity. Many patients have drug-resistant epilepsy; however, the effectiveness of VNS in this epilepsy syndrome has not been well studied.This is a single institution retrospective observational study of patients with EEM. Among a database of 134 patients with EEM, we identified those treated with VNS. Epilepsy history, VNS parameters, and response to VNS were abstracted.We identified 12 patients who were treated with VNS (50% female). The median age of epilepsy onset was 5 (range 4-14) years; age of VNS implantation was 16 (range 6-33) years, and median duration of VNS treatment was 13.5 (range 0-24) years. Four patients (33.3%) were responders reporting greater than 50% improvement in seizure frequency. All four patients (33.3%) showed response with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, myoclonic seizures, and three patients (25%) reported response with eyelid myoclonia and absence seizures. One patient had the VNS explanted due to lack of efficacy and one had it turned off for enrollment in a clinical trial. The median maximum tolerated output current settings for our cohort were 1.75 mA (IQR 1.38-1.94; range 0.75-2.25) with an OFF time of 1.8 min (IQR 1.1-3, range 0.2-3) and median duty cycle of 24% (IQR 16-29; range 12-58).From this small case series of patients with EEM, four (33.3%) were responders to VNS, with improvement noted in multiple seizure types. This indicates the potential role of VNS for patients with EEM.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Molecular Subtypes of Cholangiocarcinoma and Their Translational Implications.
abstract: Cholangiocarcinomas (CCAs) are cancers that arise in the peripheral or central bile ducts. They have substantial heterogeneity in their etiologies and histopathologic phenotypes, ranging from cholangiolar carcinomas arising from the smallest bile ducts or from dedifferentiating hepatocytes through cellular plasticity, to ductular cancers in medium and large-sized bile ducts. The surgical delineation of intrahepatic, perihilar, and distal CCAs does not match the biological classification, as intrahepatic CCAs include both small duct cholangiolar carcinoma and intermediate duct ductular or mucinous CCAs, which have different genomic and genetic characteristics. Despite their overall poor prognosis, CCAs have proven to include the most actionable target-rich types of cancer, with intrahepatic CCAs including relatively high percentages of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 fusions and isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 or 2 mutations, as well as other currently or potentially targetable aberrations. We discuss the etiologies and risk factors for CCAs, review the pathophysiologic basis for tumor molecular heterogeneity in CCA, and discuss the known links with mutational signatures in subgroups of CCA, such as oxidative stress, aging, and exogenous exposures. The potential roles of differences in cell type-specific replication timing and immunoselective and metabolic pressures are discussed, as are the implications of synergistic or antagonistic oncogenic effects, leading to unique patterns of co-occurrence vs mutual exclusivity of alterations. In addition, we review the impacts of common genetic variants and known pathogenic germline or somatic variants that predispose carriers to CCA. Finally, we discuss the role of epigenetics and variations in DNA methylation in heterogeneity of CCA within the context of evolving treatment options and remaining key gaps in knowledge.Copyright © 2026 American Gastroenterological Association Institute. title: Pulmonary Developmental Disorders in Adults: An Integrative Review of Embryology, Pathogenesis, Imaging, and Management.
abstract: Pulmonary developmental disorders comprise a heterogeneous group of congenital abnormalities involving the airways, lung parenchyma, pulmonary vasculature, or overlapping developmental pathways. Although these conditions commonly present during infancy or childhood, many remain clinically silent until adulthood, when they are discovered incidentally or manifest with recurrent respiratory symptoms such as infection, hemoptysis, or progressive dyspnea. These abnormalities may be broadly categorized into airway, vascular, parenchymal, and mixed developmental anomalies. Airway abnormalities include congenital tracheobronchomegaly, branching anomalies of the tracheobronchial tree, bronchial atresia, bronchogenic cysts, congenital pulmonary airway malformations (CPAM), and bronchopulmonary sequestration (BPS). Vascular anomalies include pulmonary artery sling, proximal interruption of the pulmonary artery, Scimitar syndrome, and meandering pulmonary veins. Parenchymal disorders encompass congenital lobar overinflation and pulmonary hypoplasia. Increasing recognition of overlapping lesions, particularly combinations of CPAM, sequestration, and bronchial atresia, has challenged traditional compartmental classification systems and supports a developmental spectrum model. This review synthesizes contemporary concepts regarding embryologic mechanisms, pathogenesis, imaging findings, and management of these entities in adults. Particular emphasis is placed on imaging evaluation with CT and MRI, updated terminology, evolving molecular understanding of CPAMs, including lesions with malignant potential, and distinctions between congenital sequestration and pseudosequestration. Recognition of these disorders and their associated anomalies is essential for accurate diagnosis, appropriate management, and surgical planning in adult patients.Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. title: The clinical utility of magnetic resonance elastography in differentiating tumor recurrence from pseudoprogression in glioblastoma.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults with nearly universal progression despite aggressive treatment. Distinguishing true tumor recurrence from treatment-related effects (pseudoprogression) remains challenging with conventional contrast-enhanced MRI, as both can produce similar imaging findings. Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), which measures tissue stiffness, has shown that gliomas are less stiff than normal brain parenchyma and that stiffness inversely correlates with tumor grade. We hypothesized that MRE could differentiate true tumor progression from treatment effects in post-treatment GBM patients. This retrospective pilot study included 13 patients with pathology-confirmed GBM who demonstrated imaging findings suspicious for recurrence on surveillance MRI. MRE was performed as an add-on sequence requiring less than 7 min of additional scan time. Regions of interest (ROIs) were manually delineated by a single neuroradiologist blinded to progression status and compared to contralateral control regions. Progression status was determined by pathologic confirmation when available or by clinical history and imaging characteristics. Among 18 analyzed lesions from 13 patients, a linear mixed effects model revealed a significant interaction between progression status (true progression or pseudoprogression) and ROI (lesion or contralateral control) on tissue stiffness (coef = -0.174 kPa, z = -12.75, p < 0.001). True tumor progression demonstrated significantly reduced stiffness compared to contralateral control tissue, while the majority of pseudoprogression lesions showed no significant stiffness reduction. MRE-derived stiffness measurements may serve as a useful imaging biomarker to distinguish GBM recurrence from treatment effects, potentially complementing perfusion MRI in guiding clinical decision-making for post-treatment GBM patients.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. title: Influence in emergency medicine: A bibliometric network analysis of the role of relationships and journals.
abstract: This study focuses on characterizing the voices that are amplified through peer reviewed publication and how they relate to one another. This study aims to 1) identify patterns of author collaboration and representation, 2) assess how this varies among different journals, 3) examine the relationship between author collaboration and quantitative publication.This is a bibliometric analysis using descriptive statistics and network analysis, examining all publications in four influential emergency medicine journals from January 2015 through December 2024. Authors and journals were assessed on quantity of publications, patterns of co-authorship, and network characteristics of individual and aggregate journals.There is a sharp right-skew of authorship - most authors have only a single article published in ten years. The most prolific authors in emergency medicine demonstrate significantly more publications than their peers. Journals show a propensity to publish multiple articles from a small number of authors, but there is variation among journals as to how many unique authors appeared during the timeframe studied. There was a gender disparity identified among the top authors, most of whom were men.Bibliometric analysis is able to demonstrate academic influence while also casting light on the role of journals in peer-reviewed publication patterns. Publication is a vital component of academic success and tangible evidence of professional influence. title: Fast Localized Calibration for Spatial-Spectral Excitation Without Fly-Back Gradients.
abstract: Standard spatial-spectral excitation pulses apply a fly-back gradient between sub-pulses, limiting, for example, how thin the slices can be (> 4 mm). Without fly-back gradients, slices can be as thin as 1.7 mm but require a phase calibration for the sub-pulses with inverted gradients due to system imperfections. Here we propose and test a fast (< 1 s), localized pre-scan enabling thin-slice frequency-selective excitation.The calibration pre-scan determines the correction phase between even and odd sub-pulses by measuring the phase difference of two FIDs excited with either the last or second-to-last RF sub-pulse of the spatial-spectral pulse. Non-localized and localized versions of the calibration pre-scan are tested and validated for water-only excitation in phantoms and the human heart. As an example, breath-held coronary MR angiography is performed with a spiral multi-slice sequence employing the proposed pulses with a slice thickness of 1.7 mm.The proposed calibration pre-scan takes 11.1 ms per slice, whether it is localized or not. Localized calibration phases are validated with an image-based calibration map. Slice profiles are visualized for pulses with different time-bandwidth products. Fat is suppressed to below 20% and 25% of the surrounding water signal in both phantoms and the human heart, respectively. High-quality coronary angiograms are demonstrated in all test subjects.Spatial-spectral pulses without fly-back gradients can be calibrated quickly (up to 90 slices in 1 s), enabling thinner slices, higher excitation angles, or pulses with sharper slice profiles using waveforms with higher time-bandwidth products.© 2026 The Author(s). title: Validation of a pan-ELastography Machine-learning (ELM) score to predict clinically significant portal hypertension in compensated advanced chronic liver disease.
abstract: The non-invasive Baveno VII criteria for clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH), based on liver stiffness measurement (LSM) and platelet count (PLT), yield indeterminate ("gray-zone") results in approximately 40-50% of patients, and their performance varies across etiologies and elastography techniques. Spleen stiffness measurement (SSM) has been proposed to improve the accuracy of the Baveno-VII CSPH criteria. We developed and validated the ELM score, a machine learning-based model integrating pan-elastographic LSM and SSM with clinical variables to improve accuracy for CSPH diagnosis, while minimizing indeterminate classifications.We analyzed 1,435 patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease who underwent paired hepatic venous pressure gradient measurements, LSM, SSM, and clinical assessment. LSM and SSM were obtained using vibration-controlled transient elastography, two-dimensional shear-wave elastography, or point shear-wave elastography. Models were trained (n = 943) and internally validated (n = 150) using harmonized elastography measurements and clinical variables. External validation was performed in 342 patients from seven centers. Cut-offs were selected to maximize rule-out and rule-in performance and compared with the Baveno VII criteria, Baveno-SSM criteria, and, in the vibration-controlled transient elastography subgroup, the ANTICIPATE and NICER scores.A random forest-based model achieved the highest performance in the external validation cohort (AUC = 0.91; Brier score = 0.13). Cut-offs of ≤0.45 (rule-out) and ≥0.60 (rule-in) yielded a negative predictive value of 0.91 (95% CI 0.84-0.95) and a positive predictive value of 0.96 (95% CI 0.92-0.98). The ELM score reduced the gray zone to 12.3%, compared with 47.9% for the Baveno VII criteria (p <0.001), 38.6% for the Baveno-SSM dual cut-off criteria (p <0.001), and 19.6% for the Baveno-SSM single cut-off criteria (p <0.05). In the vibration-controlled transient elastography external validation subgroup (n = 275), the ELM score achieved rule-in performance comparable to that of the ANTICIPATE and NICER scores while reducing the gray zone to 12.0%, compared with 38.2% and 26.5%, respectively.The ELM score outperformed the current Baveno VII criteria and substantially reduced the gray zone across elastography modalities, supporting broader and safer non-invasive identification of patients with CSPH who may benefit from non-selective beta-blocker therapy.Clinically significant portal hypertension is central to prognosis in compensated advanced chronic liver disease, yet current non-invasive strategies classify 40-50% of patients as indeterminate. This study introduces a pan-elastography machine-learning model that integrates liver and spleen stiffness with clinical variables to address this limitation. The results are important for hepatologists and healthcare systems because the ELM score reduced the diagnostic gray zone to ∼12% in external validation, compared with 47.9% for Baveno VII, while maintaining high rule-out and rule-in accuracy (NPV up to 0.91 and PPV up to 0.96). llm_summary: Researchers developed a machine-learning score called ELM that combines liver and spleen stiffness measurements with clinical information to identify patients with dangerous blood pressure buildup in the liver. The ELM score reduced uncertain diagnoses from about 48% down to 12% compared to current methods, while maintaining high accuracy for both ruling out and confirming the condition. The findings suggest this approach could help doctors more reliably identify patients who need treatment, though further testing is needed before widespread use.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers developed and validated the ELM score, a random forest machine-learning model integrating liver stiffness measurement, spleen stiffness measurement, and clinical variables to predict clinically significant portal hypertension in 1,435 patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease who underwent hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement as the reference standard. The model was trained on 943 patients, internally validated on 150 patients, and externally validated on 342 patients across seven centers using harmonized elastography measurements from multiple techniques. In external validation, the ELM score achieved an area under the curve of 0.91 with rule-out and rule-in cut-offs (≤0.45 and ≥0.60) yielding negative and positive predictive values of 0.91 and 0.96, respectively, while reducing the indeterminate gray zone to 12.3% compared with 47.9% for the Baveno VII criteria. The ELM score demonstrated superior performance to the Baveno VII, Baveno-SSM, ANTICIPATE, and NICER scores across elastography modalities and substantially reduced.

title: RF Noise Artifacts From a High Frequency Spinal Cord Stimulation System: A Retrospective Imaging Cohort With Illustrative Cases.
abstract: Unexpected RF noise artifact "followed" a patient with an implanted spinal cord stimulator to multiple MR systems. Subsequent testing and clinical scanning showed no artifact, implying that the artifact originated from the implanted device. MR exams (n = 173) performed over a two-year period in patients (n = 122) who had implanted spinal cord stimulators from the same manufacturer were reviewed for artifacts and device models. RF noise artifacts were observed in ~50% of exams in patients with a specific model of spinal cord stimulator, but only ~1%-8% of exams in other models from the same manufacturer. We hope that by describing this artifact, health care professionals can avoid service costs and scheduling delays.© 2026 International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine.

llm_summary: Researchers reviewed MRI scans from 122 patients with implanted spinal cord stimulators to identify imaging problems caused by the devices. They found that about half of the scans from patients with one specific stimulator model showed RF noise artifacts, which are unwanted visual disturbances, compared to only 1-8% of scans from other models made by the same manufacturer. Identifying this problem may help healthcare providers avoid unnecessary service calls and scheduling delays when these artifacts appear.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers reviewed 173 MR examinations performed over two years in 122 patients with implanted spinal cord stimulators from a single manufacturer to identify radiofrequency noise artifacts and their association with device models. A patient with an implanted spinal cord stimulator exhibited unexpected RF noise artifacts across multiple MR systems, and subsequent testing indicated the artifact originated from the implanted device rather than the imaging systems themselves. RF noise artifacts were observed in approximately 50% of examinations in patients with a specific spinal cord stimulator model, compared to only 1%-8% of examinations in other models from the same manufacturer. The artifact pattern suggests a device model-specific phenomenon rather than a universal characteristic of the manufacturer's spinal cord stimulation systems. This identification of model-specific imaging artifacts may help healthcare professionals avoid unnecessary service costs and scheduling delays associated with artifact investigation and repeat examinations.

title: Shared and specific associations of amygdala nuclei volumes with PTSD symptom domains and childhood trauma: An ENIGMA-PGC PTSD mega-analysis.
abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a psychiatric condition that may develop after trauma exposure. PTSD is characterized by considerable clinical heterogeneity. The amygdala's key role in fear conditioning makes it an important focus for investigating the neurobiology of PTSD. However, associations between amygdala volume and PTSD have been inconsistent. The amygdala consists of functionally distinct nuclei. Specific associations between amygdala nuclei volumes and PTSD may account for previous discrepancies between PTSD and whole amygdala volume. This study investigates the associations between amygdala nuclei volumes, PTSD diagnosis, severity, symptom cluster scores, age of onset and childhood trauma. Individuals with a PTSD diagnosis (n = 771) and controls (n = 1 081, 72% trauma-exposed) were sourced from the Enhancing Neuro-Imaging Genetics through Meta-Analysis and Psychiatric Genomics Consortium (mean age = 32.4 years, (SD = 13 years), 60% male). Nine amygdala nuclei volumes were compared to PTSD diagnosis, age of onset, overall severity, symptom cluster scores (re-experiencing, arousal, and avoidance/emotional numbing), and childhood trauma subscales. Analyses were performed using ordinary least-squares regression, corrected for age, sex, intracranial volume, and whole amygdala volume. PTSD diagnosis was not significantly associated with amygdala nuclei volumes. PTSD severity scores were associated with smaller right lateral nucleus volume (β = -0.26, pBON = 0.01). Smaller right lateral nucleus volume was also associated with re-experiencing (β = -1.01, pBON = 0.04) and arousal (β = -0.9, pBON = 0.04), smaller left paralaminar nucleus volume was associated with re-experiencing (β = -0.1, pBON = 0.04), smaller left corticoamygdaloid transition area volume was associated with avoidance (β = -0.31, pBON = 0.02). Larger left and right central nucleus volumes were significantly associated with childhood physical abuse (β = 0.24, pBON = 9 × 10-3) and neglect (β = 0.29, pBON = 0.04), respectively. Differences in select amygdala nuclei volumes among adults are associated with PTSD severity, symptom cluster scores, and childhood physical abuse and neglect. These findings demonstrate nuclei-specific patterns consistent with their functional roles in fear learning and expression.© 2026. The Author(s).

title: Global, regional, and national burden of tuberculosis and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis by HIV status, 1990-2023: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading global cause of death from a single infectious agent. Recent reductions in global health funding have threatened TB control, making comprehensive assessment of TB, HIV-related TB, and drug-resistant TB burdens before these disruptions essential for shaping effective responses. The WHO End TB Strategy sets targets of a 95% reduction in TB deaths and a 90% reduction in TB incidence between 2015 and 2035. Using results from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023, this study aims to assess the burden of TB and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) across 204 countries and territories, and to evaluate progress towards the WHO End TB incidence and mortality targets.We quantified TB mortality using the Cause of Death Ensemble modelling platform with global vital registration, surveillance, verbal autopsy, and minimally invasive tissue sampling data. For TB morbidity estimation, we simultaneously modelled incidence, prevalence, and mortality by age and sex using DisMod-MR 2.1. A population attributable fraction (PAF) approach was applied to stratify morbidity and mortality estimates by HIV and drug-resistance status. We also calculated disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) as the sum of years of life lost and years lived with disability. For the risk factor analysis, a comparative risk assessment framework was used and PAFs were derived for alcohol use, smoking, and high fasting plasma glucose to determine the proportion of TB burden associated with these risk factors.In 2023, there were an estimated 9·11 million (95% uncertainty interval 8·04-10·3) incident cases of all-form TB, 1·22 million (0·98-1·49) deaths, and 54·6 million (43·8-65·5) DALYs globally. HIV-related TB comprised 781 000 (690 000-879 000) incident cases and 210 000 (142 000-279 000) deaths, contributing 11·0 million (7·56-14·3) DALYs. MDR-TB accounted for 466 000 (198 000-1 080 000) incident cases, 102 000 (31 700-238 000) deaths, and 3·96 million (1·31-9·01) DALYs. From 2015 to 2023, global all-form TB incidence rates declined by 19·2% (17·8-20·5) and deaths declined by 22·6% (4·7-35·7); declines were larger for drug-susceptible TB than for MDR-TB. Sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia had the highest mortality burdens in 2023; reductions in all-form TB incidence and mortality were uneven between 2000 and 2023, with limited progress in both measures in Latin America and the Caribbean. Removing smoking, alcohol use, and high fasting plasma glucose would reduce global TB deaths to 768 000 (592 000-970 000) and DALYs to 34·9 million (27·8-43·8) in 2023; MDR-TB deaths would decrease to 77 200 (23 400-183 000) and DALYs to 3·12 million (1·03-7·29).Global progress towards WHO End TB targets is disparate and fragile. Although many regions achieved meaningful gains, others have stagnated in recent years. The complexity of TB prevention is amplified by divergent MDR-TB trends, the persistent burden of HIV, and growing exposure to modifiable risk factors. Recent volatility in global health financing threatens to further destabilise this vulnerable epidemiological landscape; concerted action is urgently needed to temper disruptions and preserve progress.Gates Foundation.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. llm_summary: Researchers analyzed tuberculosis burden across 204 countries from 1990 to 2023, finding that while global TB deaths declined by 23% since 2015, progress has been uneven with some regions stagnating and drug-resistant TB cases not declining as quickly as other forms. Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia carry the heaviest burden of TB deaths, and recent cuts to global health funding threaten to reverse the progress already made. The study suggests that addressing modifiable risk factors like smoking and alcohol use could substantially reduce TB deaths, but coordinated international action is urgently needed to maintain momentum toward ending the TB epidemic.
llm_summary_expert: The Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 assessed tuberculosis (TB) and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) burden across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023 using ensemble modeling of vital registration, surveillance, and verbal autopsy data, with stratification by HIV and drug-resistance status via population attributable fraction approaches. In 2023, the study estimated 9.11 million incident TB cases, 1.22 million deaths, and 54.6 million disability-adjusted life-years globally, with HIV-related TB comprising 781,000 incident cases and 210,000 deaths, and MDR-TB accounting for 466,000 incident cases and 102,000 deaths. Modifiable risk factors including smoking, alcohol use, and high fasting plasma glucose were associated.

title: Global Disparities in Insurance Coverage of Post-Mastectomy Breast Reconstruction.
abstract: Post-mastectomy breast reconstruction (PMBR) plays a critical role in restoring physical appearance and psychosocial well-being. However, pronounced geographic and socioeconomic disparities in PMBR access persist worldwide, largely driven by insurance coverage variations. We reviewed English-language literature examining regional insurance disparities in PMBR access through PubMed searches and reference screening. Access to PMBR varies dramatically across regions. Africa demonstrates the lowest utilization; fewer than 10% of eligible women undergo reconstruction, primarily through out-of-pocket payments. In Asia, South Korea's national insurance coverage achieves 77% PMBR rates, whereas limited coverage in China and India restricts access to affluent urban populations. Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and Brazil provide universal coverage with variable utilization. North America demonstrates legislative mandates in the United States, yet socioeconomic disparities persist, while Canada offers universal coverage with underutilization. title: The Society of Critical Care Cardiology-Rationale, blueprint, and lessons learned in the creation of a new multidisciplinary professional organization.
abstract: Since the cardiac intensive care unit was first introduced into the medical landscape, patient complexity, comorbidity, and illness severity have increased substantially over time. This evolution has required and informed the cultivation of new tools and an expanding skill set for those who deliver care in these units, and has paved the way for the emergence and growth of a distinct discipline-Critical Care Cardiology. With the genesis of this field and the need to care for comorbid and critically ill patients, numerous questions have been posed, including those related to optimal staffing models, appropriate training pathways, and the development of best practice principles to guide patient management. To address these and other challenges, to foster necessary collaborations, and to galvanize a maturing field, the Society of Critical Care Cardiology (SoCCC) was born.SoCCC was created to provide an independent, yet complementary home for stakeholders within this rapidly growing discipline. Its mission is to address the unique needs and concerns of Critical Care Cardiology through an inclusive approach that prioritizes the development of early career faculty, actively engaging them to help to shape the field and to strengthen its unique practice environment-the cardiac intensive care unit. While collaborations with larger professional societies remain essential, an independent subspecialty society like SoCCC intends to capitalize on the historical precedent and experiences shared by other successful organizations, while leveraging its nimble structure to advocate for and advance the needs of its constituency.While this document primarily details the history and rationale that led to the establishment of SoCCC, it also endeavors to be a practical blueprint to support future leaders who might be considering a new society for their own subspecialty.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc.
