title: Differential expression of salivary microRNA associated with keratoconus.
abstract: Research into biomarkers has transformed the identification and management of many diseases. Keratoconus (KC) is a multifactorial corneal ectasia, and due to limited understanding of disease pathophysiology, no biomarkers have been fully validated. microRNAs (miRNAs) are involved in regulating gene expression. Differentially expressed miRNAs have been reported in KC corneal tissue and as biomarkers for other ocular disorders. Salivary biomarkers mirror systemic processes and saliva contains substantial miRNAs. However, it is unknown if salivary miRNAs are differentially expressed in KC. Salivary miRNAs were collected from healthy (n = 16) and KC subjects (n = 50) and measured by qRT-PCR. Upregulated gene expression of miR-939-5p, miR-26a-5p, miR-25-3p, and miR-92a-3p; and downregulated expression of miR-320a was observed. Bioinformatic analysis using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis identified 248 experimental validated miRNA target genes and an enriched subset of 16 genes uniquely related to KC corneal functions. Gene ontology analysis demonstrated the over-representation of genes involved in protein kinase complex, protein phosphorylation, cellular senescence, apoptosis, and stress response. Our data detected previously unknown KC-dependent dysregulation of salivary miRNA expression. Future studies are warranted to determine the viability of these miRNAs as possible KC biomarkers, and to further establish their pathophysiological function.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Academic Triple Threat: Incorporating Education and Research into a Busy Colorectal Surgery Career.
abstract: The "triple threat" surgeon-one who excels as a clinician, researcher, and educator-has long represented the ultimate achievement in academic medicine. This model has guided generations of surgeons aspiring to excellence. The importance of leadership skills has also been recognized, leading to the modern concept of the "quadruple threat." Over the last decades, many challenges have threatened the existence of this model, including increasing competition for limited funding, declining reimbursement, and increasing administrative burdens. While some view the "triple threat" unachievable or unsustainable in the current environment, others use this as an opportunity to adapt the model to contemporary practice. This review examines the historical origins of the triple threat surgeon, the current challenges to this model and the steps necessary to ensure its success.Thieme. All rights reserved.

title: Single-cell sequencing reveals transcriptional and immunogenetic diversity in stereotyped chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
abstract: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) comprises immunogenetically defined stereotyped subsets of patients with distinct B-cell receptor (BcR) immunoglobulin features and clinical trajectories, yet the molecular pathways underlying subset-specific differences remain incompletely characterized. To resolve disease-relevant heterogeneity obscured in bulk analyses, we performed integrated single-cell transcriptomic and immunogenetic profiling of 48 557 malignant and bystander immune cells from 13 treatment-naïve primary patient samples representing poor-prognostic subsets #1 and #2 and the indolent subset #4. Despite interpatient variability, leukemic cells exhibited pronounced subset-specific transcriptional features, with enrichment of hypoxia-related genes in subset #1, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), MYC/E2F targets, and mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signaling in subset #2, and negative enrichment of hypoxia, apoptosis, and reactive oxygen species-related pathways in subset #4. Notably, compared with indolent subset #4, aggressive subsets #1 and #2 harbored increased proportions of metabolically active and recently emigrated/proliferative leukemic cells, characterized by a CXCR4dim CD5bright transcriptional phenotype and concerted enrichment of MYC target genes, mTORC1 signaling, OXPHOS, and BcR signaling. Immunogenetic analyses revealed dominant malignant clones with evidence of intraclonal immunogenetic diversification in 11 of 13 cases. T cells were dominated by effector-memory phenotypes exhibiting progressive differentiation toward terminal cytotoxic states, accompanied by exhaustion-associated programs, and expanded T-cell clones largely restricted to terminal states. Ligand-receptor analysis further indicated costimulatory and inhibitory signaling between leukemic and immune cells. abstract: Autoimmune hepatitis is an immune-mediated liver disease characterized by chronic inflammation and progressive fibrosis. Tissue-resident memory T cells mediate organ-specific immunity, but their role in autoimmune hepatitis remains poorly understood. title: Antiphospholipid syndrome: epidemiology and outcomes in the evolving criteria era.
abstract: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a heterogeneous autoimmune thrombo-inflammatory disorder characterized by thrombosis, pregnancy morbidity and an expanding spectrum of microvascular, cardiac, haematological and other systemic manifestations. Although research has provided considerable insights into the pathogenesis and clinical phenotypes of APS, its epidemiology remains difficult to define because estimates depend on case definitions, antibody testing, repeat-testing requirements, testing practices and data sources. Population-based studies suggest that APS is rare, and catastrophic APS is rarer and best understood through registry data. Antiphospholipid antibody positivity alone does not establish APS; transient or low-level positivity can occur without disease, whereas persistent antibodies must be interpreted alongside compatible clinical manifestations. Despite its rarity, APS causes substantial morbidity through recurrent thrombosis, organ damage and adverse pregnancy outcomes, supporting targeted evaluation in unprovoked or recurrent venous thromboembolism, stroke in younger adults and selected pregnancy complications. Apparent differences among populations can reflect ascertainment, access to testing, study design and biological variation. Standardized case definitions, antibody testing and laboratory reporting, together with longitudinal population-based research in ancestry-diverse, paediatric and low-income and middle-income populations, are needed to refine estimates of APS burden and define its clinical spectrum.© 2026. title: "It was so easy, it didn't feel real:" Positive abortion experiences post-Dobbs.
abstract: Research on abortion has disproportionately focused on legal restrictions, barriers, and stigma, contributing to a "joy deficit" in scholarship and creating epistemic foreclosures on how researchers, professionals, and abortion seekers may envision an abortion seeking experience. This study explores the positive emotions and experiences that abortion seekers had while navigating a restrictive post-Dobbs context. We conducted 81 in-depth interviews with abortion seekers from Ohio, Kentucky, and West Virginia between July 2022 and June 2025 who experienced difficulties obtaining an abortion in their state. Despite multiple financial, logistical, and emotional challenges, most participants described positive dimensions of abortion seeking, including compassionate interactions with clinic staff, practical and financial support from abortion funds, feelings of relief and joy, and unexpectedly supportive responses from friends, family, and strangers. Many participants expressed surprise at the amount of support available and lack of judgment from staff and loved ones. Positive interactions often counteracted the burdens imposed by legal and logistical barriers and, in some cases, contributed to abortion destigmatization by encouraging disclosure and normalizing abortion within social relationships. While all participants experienced barriers obtaining an abortion, most did not have solely negative experiences. The findings from this study demonstrate that abortion is a multifaceted experience, and future research efforts should focus on analyzing positive aspects of abortion seeking in restrictive settings to increase accessibility and destigmatize abortion.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. title: Trends in Magnetic Resonance Imaging Utilization and Treatment of Pediatric Tibial Spine Fractures: A National Database Study.
abstract: The management of pediatric tibial spine fractures is evolving as the evidence base has grown. Recent evidence suggests magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) evaluation may be warranted although optimal management is unknown. The present study sought to characterize national trends in surgical management and MRI utilization of pediatric tibial spine fractures.Patients aged 6-17 years presenting with a first diagnosis of closed tibial spine fracture were identified from the 2016-2022 PearlDiver M170 database. MRI utilization, treatment strategy, and surgical technique (arthroscopic reduction and internal fixation [ARIF], open reduction and internal fixation [ORIF], or anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction) were determined for each injury. Factors independently associated with these variables were assessed by a multivariable analysis. The year 2020 was excluded from analyses of trends due to changes to health care utilization during the COVID-19 pandemic.Overall, 3,554 pediatric tibial spine fracture patients were identified. MRI was obtained for 681 patients (19.1%), with independent predictors of MRI use being increased age (odds ratio [OR] ​= ​1.12 per year, P ​< ​.0001), fracture displacement (OR ​= ​2.38, P ​< ​.0001), and geographic region (Midwest relative to West, OR ​= ​1.57, P ​= ​.0013). A total of 806 patients (22.7%) underwent surgical management, with fracture displacement (OR ​= ​14.13, P ​< ​.0001) ​and preoperative MRI (OR ​= ​7.44, P ​< ​.0001) identified as independent predictors of this treatment strategy. Of patients treated surgically, ARIF was performed for 522 patients (64.8%), with an independent predictor being preoperative MRI (OR ​= ​3.00, P ​< ​.0001). Notably, the rate of MRI utilization increased significantly through the study period (15.7% in 2016, 23.1% in 2022, R2 ​= ​0.795, P ​= ​.0170), while the rates of operative treatment and ARIF did not change significantly.In this large database study of pediatric tibial spine fractures featuring over 3,000 patients treated over nearly a decade, we identified that MRI was obtained for 19.1% of the study population. The rate of MRI utilization increased over the course of the study period. Moreover, surgery was performed on 22.7% of the population. title: The Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors Journey: From Early Promise to Lasting Impact.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer therapy, yet their clinical impact is limited by immune-related adverse events (irAEs), therapeutic resistance, and the lack of reliable predictive biomarkers, contributing to a shift from early promise to a therapeutic plateau. irAEs affect multiple organ systems and may lead to treatment interruption and significant morbidity. Emerging strategies emphasize phenotype-driven and steroid-sparing approaches to control toxicity while preserving antitumor efficacy. Concurrently, primary and acquired resistance remain major challenges, driven by tumor-intrinsic mechanisms, immune microenvironment alterations, and host factors. Furthermore, current biomarkers, including programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression and tumor mutation burden, demonstrate inconsistent predictive performance across tumor types. Advances in immune profiling, genomics, and microbiome research are enabling more precise patient stratification and informing novel therapeutic strategies, including rational combinations and targeted immunomodulation. This position article synthesizes key barriers in ICI therapy while highlighting emerging opportunities to refine patient selection, improve safety, and enhance therapeutic durability. Together, these advances position the field to move beyond the current plateau toward a more precise, effective, and patient-centered era of immuno-oncology.

title: What Happens after an Incidental Thyroid Nodule? Patterns of Thyroid Ultrasound Use and Downstream Evaluation.
abstract: Incidental thyroid nodules (ITNs) detected on nonthyroid imaging contribute to thyroid cancer overdiagnosis, largely through downstream evaluation initiated by thyroid ultrasound (TUS). However, TUS follow-up rates for ITNs and their drivers in routine practice remain unclear. We quantified TUS utilization after ITN detection and identified patient, imaging, nodule, and reporting factors associated with this first step in the diagnostic cascade.We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults without prior thyroid disease who underwent imaging that incidentally captured the thyroid at Mayo Clinic sites (2017-2023). A validated natural language processing pipeline identified ITNs and extracted nodule characteristics from radiology reports across multiple imaging modalities. The main outcome was the rate of TUS within 180 days after ITN detection. Clinical outcomes, including thyroid biopsy, thyroidectomy, and thyroid cancer diagnosis, were compared between patients who underwent TUS and those who did not. Factors associated with TUS utilization were assessed using multivariable logistic regression with penalized variable selection.Among 115,683 patients who underwent thyroid-capturing imaging, 8426 (7.3%) had an ITN. These patients were predominantly female (64.6%) and White (89.7%), with a mean age of 61.7 years (standard deviation 15.2). Most nodules were detected on computed tomography (80.8%), most commonly from chest imaging (52.3%). Overall, 1677 patients with ITNs (19.9%) underwent TUS. In multivariable analysis, TUS use was independently associated with higher body mass index (odds ratio [OR], 1.20 per 10-unit increase; confidence interval [CI] [1.08-1.33]), nodule size ≥1.5 cm (OR, 1.79; CI [1.52-2.10]), and a radiologist recommendation (OR, 2.51; CI [2.12-2.98]), whereas older age was associated with lower odds of TUS (OR, 0.89 per 10-year increase; CI [0.84-0.93]). Patients undergoing TUS had higher rates of thyroid biopsy, partial thyroidectomy, and total thyroidectomy compared with those without it. All detected thyroid cancers (103 cases) occurred in the TUS group, representing 6.1% of that cohort.One in five patients with ITNs underwent TUS, representing a critical gateway to downstream diagnostic procedures and thyroid cancer detection. Factors associated with TUS utilization highlight opportunities to better define appropriateness of ultrasound after incidental nodule detection and to reduce unnecessary testing and treatment.

title: Clinical implications of the type and genomic location of pathogenic BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants in hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.
abstract: Germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (P/LPVs) in BRCA1 and BRCA2 are major determinants of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer susceptibility. Although clinical management has traditionally relied on the presence of a BRCA1/BRCA2 alteration regardless of its specific characteristics, growing evidence suggests that not all BRCA P/LPVs are biologically and clinically equivalent. Variant location within BRCA1 and BRCA2 influences the relative distribution of breast and ovarian cancer risk. Breast cancer cluster regions (BCCRs) are associated with a higher relative risk of breast versus ovarian cancer, whereas ovarian cancer cluster regions (OCCRs), largely encompassing exon 11, are associated with a relative shift toward ovarian cancer risk. Variant type may also be clinically relevant. Protein-truncating P/LPVs have been associated with higher cancer risks than selected missense variants with residual protein function and lower penetrance. Some studies have also reported poorer outcomes for carriers of protein-truncating P/LPVs and more favorable outcomes for those with missense variants. In this narrative review, we summarize current evidence on the clinical implications of BRCA1/BRCA2 P/LPV type and genomic location. While associations between variant location and breast or ovarian cancer risk are supported by large international consortia, prognostic and predictive associations remain largely exploratory. A better understanding of variant-specific genotype-phenotype correlations may ultimately refine risk prediction, preventive strategies, and treatment selection in hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. llm_summary: This review examined how different types of BRCA gene mutations affect breast and ovarian cancer risk in people with hereditary cancer susceptibility. Researchers found that the location and type of mutation matter: mutations in certain regions increase breast cancer risk while others increase ovarian cancer risk, and mutations that completely disable the protein cause higher cancer risks than those with partial function. While these patterns are well-established for predicting cancer risk, the evidence for how they affect treatment outcomes and survival remains preliminary and needs further study.
llm_summary_expert: This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on how the type and genomic location of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (P/LPVs) in BRCA1 and BRCA2 influence clinical outcomes in hereditary breast and ovarian cancer. Variant location within these genes demonstrates clinically relevant associations with cancer risk distribution, with breast cancer cluster regions (BCCRs) associated with higher relative breast cancer risk and ovarian cancer cluster regions (OCCRs), largely encompassing exon 11, associated with a relative shift toward ovarian cancer risk. Protein-truncating P/LPVs have been associated with higher cancer risks compared to selected missense variants with residual protein function and lower penetrance, and some studies report poorer outcomes for carriers of protein-truncating variants and more favorable outcomes for those with missense variants. While associations between variant location and breast or ovarian cancer risk are supported by large international consortia, the prognostic and predictive associations of variant type remain largely exploratory. Improved understanding of variant-specific genotype-phenotype correlations may refine risk prediction, preventive strategies, and treatment selection in hereditary breast and ovarian.

title: Diagnostic delay and poor functional outcomes in late-onset NMOSD: A Thai cohort study.
abstract: Late-onset neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (LONMOSD) may be difficult to recognize because symptoms can mimic other neurological disorders in older patients. Data on LONMOSD in Thailand remain limited.To compare clinical characteristics and outcomes between early-onset NMOSD (EONMOSD) and LONMOSD in a Thai cohort, and to evaluate the impact and causes of delayed diagnosis in LONMOSD.We retrospectively studied adult patients with NMOSD who fulfilled the 2015 International Panel for NMO Diagnosis criteria at a tertiary referral center in Thailand from 2016 to 2025. LONMOSD was defined as onset at age ≥50 years. Clinical characteristics, treatment, Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), relapse outcomes, and reasons for delayed diagnosis were analyzed.Among 148 patients, 91 had EONMOSD and 57 had LONMOSD. LONMOSD was associated with more frequent delayed diagnosis than EONMOSD (54.4%vs 31.9%, P = 0.01). LONMOSD patients had higher EDSS at nadir, 90 days, and 180 days, and lower recovery index at 180 days. Relapse outcomes and time to subsequent relapse were not significantly different between groups. In LONMOSD, myelitis was independently associated with EDSS ≥6 at 90 and 180 days, while delayed diagnosis was associated with EDSS ≥6 at 90 days. Misdiagnosis was the main cause of delayed diagnosis, most commonly cerebrovascular disease and compressive myelopathy.LONMOSD was associated with delayed diagnosis and worse functional outcomes. Early recognition may reduce preventable disability in older patients.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers compared older patients with a rare neurological disorder called neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) to younger patients, finding that older patients experienced delayed diagnosis more than twice as often and had worse physical function at multiple time points. The delayed diagnoses were mainly caused by doctors mistakenly identifying the condition as stroke or spinal compression instead. Early recognition of NMOSD in older adults may help prevent unnecessary disability.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers conducted a retrospective cohort study of 148 adult patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) diagnosed at a Thai tertiary center between 2016 and 2025, comparing 57 patients with late-onset NMOSD (LONMOSD, age ≥50 years) to 91 with early-onset NMOSD (EONMOSD) using the 2015 International Panel for NMO Diagnosis criteria. The primary endpoints were diagnostic delay, Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores at nadir and 90 and 180 days, recovery index at 180 days, and relapse outcomes. LONMOSD was associated with significantly higher rates of delayed diagnosis compared to EONMOSD (54.4% versus 31.9%), higher EDSS scores at nadir and at 90 and 180 days, and lower recovery index at 180 days, while relapse outcomes and time to subsequent relapse did not differ significantly between groups. In LONMOSD patients, myelitis was independently associated with EDSS.

title: mRNA-engineered stem cells produce nerve growth factor and induce neurite outgrowth in recipient cells.
abstract: Innervation is essential for tissue healing, yet strategies to enhance nerve growth during repair remain limited. Here, we show that chemically modified messenger RNA (cmRNA) encoding nerve growth factor (NGF) can stimulate neurogenic responses in vitro. NGF cmRNA was delivered to human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells using lipid carriers, leading to efficient NGF production. In co-culture, NGF-secreting stem cells induced differentiation of neural crest-derived PC-12 cells, as evidenced by increased neurite outgrowth and branching. Proteomic analyses revealed activation of neurogenesis-related pathways in both cell types. Notably, NGF cmRNA-transfected stem cells produced lower NGF levels than recombinant protein yet achieved comparable neurite-outgrowth response, demonstrating the efficiency of the transcript-based approach. These findings demonstrate that NGF cmRNA can induce NGF production by hMSCs and promote neurite outgrowth in NGF-responsive PC12 cells in vitro. This approach may provide the neurotrophic component of future regenerative strategies combining NGF cmRNA with osteogenic signals; however, its effects on functional tissue innervation and bone healing remain to be established in vivo.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. When these modified stem cells were grown alongside nerve cells, they successfully triggered nerve cell differentiation and outgrowth, achieving results comparable to using purified nerve growth factor protein directly. While this approach shows promise for future tissue repair strategies, its effectiveness in actual bone healing and nerve function in living organisms still needs to be tested.

title: From 5 to 15: The Impact of Increased Program Signals in the 2024 to 2025 General Surgery Application Cycle.
abstract: To evaluate the change from 5 program signals to 15 program signals in General Surgery using data from the 2024 to 2025 cycle using AAMC ERAS® application, Thalamus interview, and NRMP ranking and matching data.Data collected by the NNBME, AAMC, Thalamus, and NRMP were analyzed to assess the impact of program signals on: interview invitation, placement on a program's rank order list (ROL), ranking in the top quartile of a program's ROL, and applicants matching into programs.The 2024 to 2025 residency application cycle.Applicants applying to and ranking programs in General Surgery during the 2024 to 2025 residency application cycle.A significant decrease in the average number of applications per applicant between the 2024 and the 2025 cycle was noted. Candidates were more likely to get an interview invitation and be placed on a program's ROL at a program they signaled when compared to a program they did not signal. Signaling positively impacted candidate median match rate.These data suggest that program signals are being used by both applicants and programs to help place the right applicant in the right program. The shift to large number of signals may have encouraged applicants to submit fewer applications and it did not negatively impact interview or match outcomes. Ongoing research in this area is critical to better understand the impacts of program signaling on residency and resident selection and to assess any unintended negative consequences.Copyright © 2026 Association of Program Directors in Surgery. llm_summary: Researchers examined how increasing program signals—indicators of mutual interest between applicants and residency programs—from 5 to 15 affected General Surgery residency placements during the 2024 to 2025 application cycle. Applicants who signaled interest in a program were significantly more likely to receive interview invitations and be ranked favorably, and the change was associated with fewer total applications submitted per candidate without harming match outcomes. The findings suggest that program signals help match applicants with suitable programs, though researchers note that further study is needed to identify any unintended negative effects.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers evaluated the impact of increasing program signals from 5 to 15 in the 2024 to 2025 General Surgery residency application cycle using data from AAMC ERAS, Thalamus interview platform, and NRMP matching records. The study analyzed associations between program signaling and four outcomes: interview invitation rates, placement on program rank order lists, ranking in the top quartile of lists, and match success among applicants applying to and ranking General Surgery programs. Applicants who signaled a program were significantly more likely to receive interview invitations and be placed on that program's rank order list compared to programs they did not signal, and signaling was associated with improved median match rates. The average number of applications per applicant decreased between the 2024 and 2025 cycles, yet this reduction did not negatively impact interview or match outcomes. These findings suggest that program signals facilitate better matching between applicants and programs, though ongoing research is needed to identify any unintended negative consequences of the expanded signaling system.

title: Reframing the Gut-Brain Axis: The Gut Wall as a Neural Immune Interface in Multiple Sclerosis and Autoimmune Neurological Diseases.
abstract: Gut wall physiology in multiple sclerosis (MS) and autoimmune neurologic diseases remains underexplored. This review examines gut wall dysfunctions' contribution to MS and autoimmune neurological disorder pathogenesis and progression. We discuss 3 inter-related aspects of gut physiology: intestinal barrier, enteric nervous system (ENS), and mucosal immunity. We highlight the ENS as a putative target of immune injury in selected antibody-mediated and T cell-associated neurologic diseases. Finally, we propose a unifying framework in which the gut functions as a site of immune priming and target of autoimmune injury, bridging microbiome-driven mechanisms in MS with ENS-directed autoimmunity across neurologic diseases. The authors propose that the gut serves as both a place where immune responses are triggered and a target of autoimmune attack, potentially linking gut bacteria changes to nerve-directed autoimmunity across various neurological conditions. This framework suggests the gut wall functions as a critical interface between immune and nervous system dysfunction in these diseases.

title: Episodic hypercortisolemia-mediated periods of worsening hyperglycemia in cyclic Cushing syndrome.
abstract: Cyclic Cushing syndrome (CCS) is a rare subtype of Cushing syndrome (CS) characterized by hypercortisolism alternating with periods of physiologic or even low cortisol secretion. Most patients with CCS present with clinical signs of CS; however, in some patients, signs of hypercortisolism may be subtle or even absent. The fluctuating clinical picture and discrepant biochemical findings make CCS difficult to diagnose. We describe a case of a 70-year-old man with well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus who experienced recurrent, spontaneous hypercortisolemic episodes resulting in worsening and difficult-to-control hyperglycemia, followed by eucortisolemic phases during which his glycemic control rapidly returned to baseline. Further biochemical evaluation revealed intermittent hypercortisolemia without a clearly identifiable source of an adrenocorticotropic hormone secreting lesion. Data from his continuous glucose monitoring system (CGMS) proved pivotal in detecting the hypercortisolemic phases and tailoring management. After declining bilateral adrenalectomy and opting for a block-and-replace regimen with osilodrostat and hydrocortisone, he was able to anticipate and initiate this treatment based on his CGMS readings, facilitating improved glycemic control during these periods. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of CCS and the utility of CGMS as both a monitoring tool and treatment guide for CCS in patients with concurrent type 2 diabetes mellitus.© The Author(s) 2026. Using continuous glucose monitoring to track blood sugar patterns, doctors identified when these hormone surges occurred and helped the patient manage them with medication rather than surgery. This case demonstrates how glucose monitoring can help diagnose and treat this rare condition in patients with diabetes.
llm_summary_expert: This case report describes a 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus who presented with cyclic Cushing syndrome (CCS), a rare condition characterized by alternating periods of hypercortisolemia and normal or low cortisol secretion. title: PET/MR Imaging of the Gastrointestinal Tract.
abstract: PET/MR imaging combines molecular PET data with multiparametric MR imaging in a single reduced-radiation examination of the gastrointestinal tract. For oncologic indications, the hybrid modality adds value in hepatic metastasis detection, locoregional staging, and posttreatment response assessment. Radiotracers beyond fluorodeoxyglucose, including fibroblast activation protein inhibitor ligands and somatostatin receptor analogs, expand diagnostic reach in tumors with low glycolytic activity and in neuroendocrine disease. For inflammatory bowel disease, PET/MR enterography assists with selected questions such as differentiation of inflammatory from fibrotic strictures. title: A proliferation score defined by PCLI-anchored transcriptomics predicts outcomes in multiple myeloma.
abstract: Cell proliferation is a fundamental driver of disease aggressiveness in multiple myeloma (MM); however, transcriptional programs underpinning proliferative capacity remain incompletely defined. Using Affymetrix microarray data from 136 Mayo Clinic patients with MM with paired plasma cell labeling index (PCLI), we performed a differential expression analysis to identify genes consistently associated with proliferative activity. These genes were subsequently incorporated into the development of a prognostic model using baseline RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) profiles in purified CD138+ cells from 656 patients in the CoMMpass cohort, in which an elastic net-based Cox model yielded an 8-gene-based proliferation score (GPS). Differential expression analysis identified 108 proliferation-associated genes, and the resulting 8-gene GPS (CHEK1, EXO1, MCM4, TK1, KIF14, SEPTIN11, PHF19, and HMGB3) formed a highly connected biological network enriched for DNA damage response and cell cycle regulation. CHEK1, TK1, EXO1, and MCM4 were mapped in a large network with CHEK1 as the hub gene. In the CoMMpass data set, on dividing the GPS score by the median, the high-GPS group (n = 328) had a median overall survival (OS) of 63.6 months (95% confidence interval, 56.5-76.7), whereas the low-GPS group (n = 328) had a median OS of 106.1 months (P < .001). Similarly, in another Mayo Clinic RNA-seq cohort, high-GPS group (n = 12) demonstrated worse survival (median OS, 39.2 vs 157.1 months for the low-GPS group; P = .03). title: Circulating Nephrin Antibodies and Post-Transplant Recurrence of Diffuse Podocytopathies: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Recurrence of diffuse podocytopathy (DP), primarily focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and minimal change disease, after kidney transplantation threatens allograft survival. Circulating nephrin autoantibodies have been linked to disease activity, but posttransplant evidence remains limited. We performed a systematic review with patient-level data extraction, including kidney transplant recipients with DP as their native kidney disease from studies reporting serum nephrin antibody testing and posttransplant outcomes. Four studies including 63 recipients (23 pediatric and 40 adult) with DP were included, comprising 53 focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, 8 minimal change disease, and 2 steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome cases. Nephrin antibodies were detected in 22 of 62 tested recipients (36%), either before transplantation or during posttransplant recurrence, including one patient in whom antibodies were detected 9 years after transplantation. Recurrence occurred in 34 of 63 recipients (54%), including 20 of 22 (91%) antibody-positive patients. Antibody positivity was strongly associated with recurrence (OR 20.8; 95% CI, 4.2-102.6; P < 0.001), with sensitivity of 61%, specificity of 93%, positive predictive value of 91%, and negative predictive value of 68%. Antibody titers correlated with disease activity and declined with remission. Nephrin autoantibodies are associated with posttransplant recurrence of DP and may inform pretransplant risk stratification and posttransplant monitoring. Standardized assays and larger validation studies are needed.© 2026 The Authors.

title: A Pilot Study to Describe Symptomatic Hyperammonemia Secondary to Recombinant Erwinia Asparaginase.
abstract: Asparaginase therapy is essential for the treatment of pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (ALL/LLy). For patients who develop hypersensitivity to a first-line Escherichia coli (E. coli)-derived product, the standard of care is to transition to an Erwinia-derived product. Given that all asparaginase products exert their antileukemic effects by enzymatically breaking down asparagine to aspartic acid and ammonia, elevations in ammonia levels are anticipated during asparaginase treatment. However, symptomatic hyperammonemia is not expected. Recombinant Erwinia asparaginase is relatively new to the market, and there have been several case reports of symptomatic hyperammonemia with this specific formulation.The primary objective of this prospective study was to establish the incidence of symptomatic hyperammonemia secondary to recombinant Erwinia asparaginase and to determine if a larger, multicenter trial was warranted. Additional objectives included identifying potential risk factors for symptomatic hyperammonemia.This single-center, prospective trial received institutional review board approval. Funding was provided by the Mayo Clinic Clinical and Translational Science Award (grant number: UL1TR002377) and the Mayo Clinic Department of Pharmacy. All patients treated by the pediatric hematology/oncology team at our institution who were receiving recombinant Erwinia asparaginase were eligible. Patients were excluded if they were less than 1 year of age at study entry. Enrolled participants had a baseline plasma ammonia level obtained, followed by twice weekly ammonia levels while receiving recombinant Erwinia asparaginase. Aside from baseline, all ammonia levels were trough levels measured either 48 h or 72 h after the previous dose.Five patients were included, three of whom were male (60%). Three patients had T-cell ALL (60%), one patient had B-cell ALL (20%), and one patient had infantile B-cell ALL (20%). The median age was 5 years (range 1-14). Two patients were followed for two courses of recombinant Erwinia asparaginase, and the remaining patients were followed for a single course. Median baseline plasma ammonia level was 12 μmol/L. Median ammonia level while receiving recombinant Erwinia asparaginase was 146 μmol/L. Three patients (60%) developed symptomatic hyperammonemia with a median ammonia level of 174 μmol/L (range 108-343). The reported symptoms were nausea (100%), fatigue (66.7%), and decreased appetite (33.3%). The remaining two patients experienced asymptomatic hyperammonemia with a median ammonia level of 125 μmol/L (range 55-304).Based on our small cohort, symptomatic hyperammonemia may be a common adverse effect for patients receiving recombinant Erwinia asparaginase. Evaluating plasma ammonia levels appears reasonable in patients who are experiencing nausea or other symptoms of hyperammonemia. title: Vascular Abnormalities in the Hand and Wrist: State-of-the-Art Multimodality Imaging.
abstract: Vascular abnormalities are less common in the hand and wrist than in the lower extremities but can result in significant morbidity if unrecognized or untreated. The unique vascular architecture of the hand and wrist, with a dense network of arterial anastomoses, confers resilience to ischemia, but the superficial location makes them vulnerable to trauma and occupational injury. The authors describe and illustrate a comprehensive multimodality imaging approach to the diagnosis and evaluation of vascular abnormalities of the hand and wrist. They begin with an overview of vascular anatomy and normal variants, including a persistent median artery. Multimodality imaging, including US, CT angiography, MR angiography, and digital subtraction angiography, is reviewed with a focus on strengths, limitations, and clinical utility. Dynamic imaging techniques and photon-counting CT are highlighted for their evolving roles. A wide spectrum of vascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, trauma, iatrogenic injury, embolism, hypothenar hammer syndrome, hand-arm vibration syndrome, vasculitis, and frostbite, as well as their imaging appearances, are discussed. Vascular anomalies, including vascular malformations and vascular neoplasms, are also reviewed. The role of imaging in hand transplantation is addressed. The authors provide a framework for recognizing vascular diseases in the hand and wrist and selecting the appropriate imaging modality. Familiarity with vascular anatomy, imaging findings, and clinical context is essential for timely diagnosis, guiding management, and preserving limb function.©RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article.

title: GABAergic Network Dysregulation in Alcohol Use Disorder: Receptor-Transporter Interactions Driving the Transition From Goal-Directed to Compulsive Behaviour.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is characterized by a shift from controlled, goal-directed drinking to compulsive, habitual alcohol (a.k.a. ethanol) seeking, even in the face of negative outcomes. This transition is closely associated with alterations in cortico-striatal circuitry and dysregulated GABAergic signalling, both of which drive the progression from flexible control to compulsive behaviour. Acute alcohol exposure enhances GABAergic inhibition, primarily by increasing presynaptic GABA release. Chronic exposure leads to compensatory neuroadaptations, such as subunit reorganization, receptor internalization and diminished GABA receptor sensitivity. While these neuroadaptations alter receptor-mediated GABAergic signalling during dependence and withdrawal, they also alter dopaminergic regulation and further reinforce alcohol-seeking behaviour. Beyond receptor-level adaptations, impaired GABA clearance, especially through the astrocytic transporter GAT3, plays a crucial role in regulating extracellular GABA concentrations and tonic inhibition. This effect is particularly evident within the dorsal striatum, where elevated tonic GABA shifts control from flexible, goal-directed action towards rigid, habitual responding by altering the balance between the dorsomedial and dorsolateral subregions. Consistent with these mechanistic insights, animal and human studies demonstrate that reduced GAT3 expression is associated with compulsive alcohol use and impaired reward-related behaviour, reinforcing impaired GABA clearance as a central mechanism in this behavioural shift. Taken together, these lines of evidence validate a central therapeutic model, namely, that targeting altered tonic inhibition and impaired GABA clearance in AUD could address the inhibitory dysfunction that sustains the disorder. Overall, this work supports a unifying model in which receptor adaptations and disrupted GABA removal maintain altered inhibitory tone, driving maladaptive circuit function and contributing to the persistence of AUD.© 2026 The Author(s). title: Living Liver Donors With Obesity and Metabolic Risk: Review and Guidance on Donor Triage and Care.
abstract: With the increasing prevalence of obesity in the United States, potential living liver donors (LLDs) are similarly impacted. Historically, LLDs with obesity are deemed too high risk for donation due to concern for hepatic steatosis (HS) or post-surgical complications. Evolving data show that obesity is not the absolute indicator of HS and metabolic risk. Instead, distribution of fat in the visceral area as well as body composition drive the risk for metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Prior practice patterns of denial of obese LLDs with metabolic risk require a change in mindset from the liver transplant community with a thoughtful, individualized risk assessment of all LLDs. By losing weight utilizing various dietary and procedural strategies, these "gray zone" LLDs improve their metabolic risk profile and can move into a low risk "green zone", thus expanding the donor pool. Little data exist whether "gray zone" LLDs who succeed in weight loss have long-term consequences to their own health if they regain their weight or the clinical impact on their LDLT recipients. Ethical and financial questions remain as to the LDLT centers' direct responsibility to maintaining donor health. llm_summary: Researchers reviewed how obesity affects living liver donors and found that obesity alone does not necessarily make someone too risky to donate, since the location of body fat and overall body composition matter more for liver health. Donors classified as higher risk can potentially move to lower risk categories through weight loss using diet and other strategies, which could expand the available donor pool. However, important questions remain about whether donors who lose weight and then regain it experience long-term health problems and how this affects transplant recipients.
llm_summary_expert: This review examines the evaluation and management of living liver donors with obesity and metabolic risk, challenging the historical practice of categorically excluding obese donors based solely on body mass index. The authors argue that visceral fat distribution and body composition, rather than obesity alone, are the primary drivers of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and post-surgical complications in potential donors. The paper proposes an individualized risk assessment approach that stratifies donors into risk categories, with "gray zone" donors potentially improving their metabolic profile through weight loss interventions and dietary or procedural strategies to transition into a low-risk "green zone. " This approach could expand the living donor liver transplant pool by identifying suitable candidates previously denied based on obesity status alone. The authors identify critical gaps in knowledge regarding long-term health consequences for donors who lose weight preoperatively but regain it postoperatively, as well as the clinical impact on recipients, and call for future studies to evaluate interventions and outcomes alongside clarification of transplant centers' ethical and financial responsibilities for donor health maintenance.

title: Characterizing bone metastases and skeletal-related events in patients with well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasms utilizing 68Gallium-DOTATATE positron emission tomography.
abstract: Tumors of neuroendocrine origin are a heterogenous group of related neoplasms which can arise from anywhere in the body. Neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) are categorized by site of origin, differentiation status and grade (Ki-67 expression and/or mitotic rate), with significant prognostic variability accordingly. Historically, the prevalence of bone metastasis is reported to be 6%-12% based on "first generation" (i.e., 111Indium pentetreotide [Octreoscan®]) somatostatin receptor imaging (SSRI). We conducted a retrospective cohort study including patients with well-differentiated NENs to determine the clinical and imaging characteristics of osseous metastases when evaluated with higher-sensitivity 68Gallium-DOTATATE positron emission tomography (PET) scans, as well as determining fracture prevalence in selected sub-cohorts. We also developed a risk score analysis to assess risk of fracture in this cohort. Four hundred twenty-four patients were identified for inclusion. The median age was 61 years. Most patients were asymptomatic (64%), had sclerotic lesions (77%), Krenning 4 (71%), and had >3 sites (69%) of osseous disease. A high proportion of patients had osseous metastases at sites with high risk for fracture, including vertebra (82%), pelvis (63%), and peri-trochanteric femur (34%). Fifty-seven patients (13%) in the entire cohort suffered a fracture. Fracture prevalence was significantly lower in small bowel neuroendocrine tumors (NETs, 7%) and Grades 1 and 2 disease (8% and 9%, respectively), with higher prevalence in pancreatic NETs, paragangliomas/pheochromocytomas, lung carcinoid, and Grade 3 disease (≥20% for each; p-values <.05). Our study showed that the rate of osseous metastatic disease approximates 20% in well-differentiated NENs. Most bone metastases are asymptomatic and the risk of fracture is variable based on the primary site of disease and tumor grade. Our novel risk score analysis for fracture was designed to assist clinician decision making as to management of bone metastasis in this patient population.© 2026 The Author(s). title: Development of the Children's Oncology Group long-term follow-up guideline for cancer genetics evaluation in childhood cancer survivors.
abstract: Up to 12% of childhood cancer survivors have an underlying cancer predisposition syndrome (CPS). As a result, these childhood cancer survivors are at increased risk for developing and succumbing to subsequent malignant neoplasms. Identifying childhood cancer survivors with CPS is essential to improving overall outcomes by informing tailored approaches to cancer screening, treatment, and, for some, risk-reducing interventions. Despite these potential benefits, it is often unclear which childhood cancer survivors warrant referral for genetic counselling and germline genetic testing. Using an evidence-based approach, a standardised guideline for referral for cancer genetics evaluation of childhood cancer survivors at high risk of having a CPS was developed and incorporated into the Children's Oncology Group Long-Term Follow-Up Guidelines for Survivors of Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancers. This Policy Review details the importance, development, and anticipated impact of this new guideline. Raising awareness of this guideline is crucial to enhancing the integration of genetics into survivorship care and improving health outcomes for childhood cancer survivors with CPS.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Differential contributions of CO2 and blood pressure to cerebral macro- and microvascular reactivity in healthy adults.
abstract: Cerebrovascular reactivity to CO2 (CVR-CO2) is widely used to assess cerebrovascular function, yet it remains unclear how changes in upstream arterial inflow and downstream microvascular oxygenation are coupled during CO2 perturbations, and how concurrent blood pressure (BP) changes modulate these responses. We aimed to quantify macro- and microvascular CVR-CO2 while disentangling the relative and independent contributions of BP and CO2 during hypo- and hypercapnic stimuli. In 41 healthy adults, including 21 female participants, macrovascular blood flow velocity (CBFV; transcranial Doppler) and microvascular oxygenation (oxyhemoglobin; near-infrared spectroscopy) were recorded during hyperventilation-induced hypocapnia and rebreathing-induced hypercapnia. Hypocapnic reactivity was assessed using linear regression of changes in end-tidal CO2 and BP, while hypercapnic responses were analyzed breath-by-breath using linear mixed-effects models. During hypocapnia, CO2 was the primary driver of both macrovascular and microvascular responses, with negligible BP contributions and only modest macro- and micro-CVR-CO2 correlations. In contrast, during hypercapnia, while CO2 remained dominant, macro- and micro-CVR-CO2 correlations were absent; BP contributed proportionally more to macrovascular than to microvascular responses. These findings indicate that BP independently influences CVR-CO2 during hypercapnia and that microvascular responses to CO2 diverge from upstream arterial inflow. Recognizing these differential vascular responses to CO2 improves interpretations of CVR-CO2 metrics and likely informs individualized assessment of cerebrovascular function.NEW & NOTEWORTHY This study indicates that cerebrovascular reactivity to CO2 (CVR-CO2) differs between the macro- and microcirculation during both hypocapnia and hypercapnia and that relative contributions of CO2 and blood pressure to these responses differ between vascular compartments during hypercapnia. These findings highlight the importance of considering compartment-specific regulatory mechanisms when interpreting CVR-CO2.

title: Blood- and Liver Stiffness-Based Non-Invasive Tests for Clinically Significant Portal Hypertension in Patients With cACLD and HCC.
abstract: The applicability of non-invasive tests (NITs) for clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is controversial. We performed a head-to-head comparison of various NITs for CSPH and evaluated rule-in/-out criteria.We conducted a retrospective study including 283 patients with HCC undergoing hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) measurement at the Vienna Hepatic Haemodynamic Lab with available, same-day data on NITs (i.e., liver stiffness measurement [LSM], platelet count [PLT], von Willebrand factor antigen [VWF:Ag], and the ratio of VWF:Ag and PLT [VITRO]). For the subsequent analysis, we focused on patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease (cACLD).Among 164 patients with cACLD, most were BCLC 0/A (50.6%) and CSPH prevalence was 46.3%, the median LSM was 20.0 kPa (IQR: 13.3-37.9), and mean VWF:Ag/VITRO was 266 ± 119%/2.30 ± 1.81. The VITRO score yielded the highest discriminative ability to detect CSPH (AUROC: 0.834), followed by ANTICIPATE ± NASH (AUROC: 0.822), PLT (AUROC: 0.803), LSM (AUROC: 0.779), and VWF:Ag (AUROC: 0.707). The application of the Baveno VII criterium (LSM ≤ 15 kPa & PLT ≥ 150G/L) and the VITRO score (≤ 1.0) individually showed an excellent performance for ruling-out CSPH (sensitivities: ≥ 95%, NPV: 100%/87.9%). For ruling-in CSPH by individual criteria, the VITRO score provided the highest PPV (≥ 2.5, specificity/PPV: 89.8%/83.0%), followed by the Baveno VII criteria (specificity/PPV: 81.8%/74.6%). When sequentially applying Baveno VII criteria and VITRO, the grey zone could be significantly reduced to 16% (sensitivity/NPV: 94.7%/92.2%; specificity/PPV: 73.9%/84.4%).The discriminative ability in patients with cACLD and HCC was comparable to patients without HCC. However, PPVs of established criteria were < 90%, which may be explained by the comparatively low prevalence of CSPH in this context.© 2026 The Author(s). title: Efficiently harvesting low-energy photons from silicon photon counting detectors.
abstract: X-rays incident on silicon photon counting detectors (Si PCDs) may undergo Compton scattering and deposit only a few keV of energy into the sensor. These events are difficult to distinguish from electronic noise. Prior to reconstruction, the scanner must solve a hybrid estimation problem to determine attenuation, in which the lowest energy bin is corrupted by false counts, but the upper energy bins are essentially immune to electronic noise.To efficiently estimate attenuation in this hybrid scenario. Prior authors have considered attenuation estimation with PCDs that are fully immune to electronic noise, or in energy-integrating detectors that include electronic noise, but the optimal estimator in the hybrid scenario remains unknown. The purpose of this work is to design such an attenuation estimator that reduces bias and variance in Si-PCD CT images.We propose to use convex optimization to build a 2D-lookup table that maps counts using the lowest energy bin (containing false counts) and the upper bins (all counts grouped together as a single bin, free of false counts) to the best estimated object attenuation. The energy thresholds of the Si PCD were selected to be 6 and 10 keV using assumptions from the literature. In the regime of interest, counts are scarce, so both false counts and true counts were modeled as Poisson. Our proposed estimator was compared with three reference estimators: naive logarithm estimator and modified logarithm estimators based on Li et al. (IEEE Trans Med Img 2023) and Bushe et al. (Phys Med Biol 2023). The reference estimators were applied using either both lowest and upper bins, or using upper bins only. 20-, 30- and 40- cm water phantoms, containing two 2.6-cm bone-like inserts, were tested in simulation. We assumed a technique of 120 kVp and 833 mA without mA modulation. To avoid confounding artifacts from beam hardening, the bone-like inserts were modeled as being water-equivalent in atomic number but high density, and a water beam hardening correction was used.The proposed estimator achieved zero average bias and the lowest variance across all phantom sizes when compared to the reference estimators. When using both energy bins for the 30-cm phantom, the logarithm, Li's, and Bushe's estimators had biases of 4, 1, and 1 HU and variances that were 7%, 5%, and 5% higher than the proposed method, respectively, in the area between the two inserts. For the 40-cm phantom, their biases increased to over 20 HU. Conversely, when using only the upper energy bins for the 30-cm phantom, the logarithm, Li's, and Bushe's estimators had biases of 4, 0, and 0 HU but with significant increase in variance to 17%, 14%, and 14% higher than our estimator, respectively, and still produced bias on the 40-cm phantom.For Si PCDs, setting the lowest energy threshold low enough to detect at least some false counts in combination with our proposed attenuation estimator can improve dose efficiency for non-spectral imaging tasks.© 2026 American Association of Physicists in Medicine.

title: The Pros & Cons of Measuring Plasma Ammonia in the Management of Patients With Cirrhosis: An ISHEN Debate.
abstract: Ammonia is a nitrogenous molecule which is primarily generated in the gastrointestinal tract. The neurotoxicity of ammonia plays a critical role in the liver's regulation of circulating ammonia levels. In liver disease, an increase in blood ammonia has been long implicated in the pathogenesis of hepatic encephalopathy (HE), a neurological complication of liver disease. However, the clinical value of measuring plasma ammonia in patients with cirrhosis remains controversial. This dilemma was the subject of a debate held at the International Society of Hepatic Encephalopathy and Nitrogen Metabolism (ISHEN) meeting in St-Paulin, Québec, Canada in October 2025. This review illustrates the pros & cons of measuring plasma ammonia in the management of patients with cirrhosis.© 2026 The Author(s). Liver International published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

title: Results from the VANISH study: A prospective multicenter study validating a single-nucleotide polymorphism-based noninvasive prenatal test to assess aneuploidy risk in surviving twins of vanishing twin pregnancies.
abstract: To develop and validate a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based noninvasive prenatal cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening algorithm capable of identifying the cfDNA signal of the living fetus in vanishing twin (VT) pregnancies and assessing that twin's aneuploidy risk.Prospective study enrolling participants ≥18 years old at ≥9 weeks' gestation with an ultrasound-confirmed VT at 21 US sites (August 2021 to August 2023). The study protocol specified SNP-based cfDNA screening at enrollment and at two additional 3-week intervals. Neonatal buccal swabs evaluated the SNP profile of the living fetus. Cases lost to follow-up and with missing samples were excluded. Using SNP-based technology, an algorithm to identify the living fetus was developed based on the number of fetoplacental cfDNA signals and individual fetal fraction measurements. Concordance between cfDNA in maternal plasma and newborn buccal-swab SNP profiles was used to validate the algorithm in correctly identifying the living fetus. Common aneuploidies and fetal sex were determined for the living fetus.Of 136 participants enrolled, 106 met criteria for the final analysis; 45 for development and 61 for validation. In the validation cohort, median gestational age was 10.7 weeks (range: 8.0-16.1 weeks) at ultrasound diagnosis of a VT. In 93.4% of validation cases, the algorithm identified the living fetus and gave an aneuploidy result; 90.2% within the first two blood draws. At the time the living fetus was identified, 39 samples had two fetoplacental signals and 18 had one. Aneuploidy results included 56 low-risk and one high-risk result for trisomy 21. Neonatal buccal swabs confirmed that the VT algorithm correctly identified the living twin and gave a correct aneuploidy result in 57/57 cases (100%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 93.5%, 100.0%). Among 29 participants with all three blood draws and two fetoplacental signals at enrollment, two signals persisted in 93.1% at the second blood draw and 72.4% at the third.The SNP-based algorithm accurately identified the living fetus in VT pregnancies in this small study. title: Application of Optic Neuritis Diagnostic Criteria in Autoimmune Paraneoplastic CRMP5 Optic Neuropathy and Development of the "CRMP" Score.
abstract: Collapsin response-mediator protein 5 (CRMP5)-IgG is an acknowledged biomarker in the International Consortium on Optic Neuritis (ICON) diagnostic criteria for optic neuritis (ON), but these criteria have not been validated in CRMP5-IgG+ON.We evaluated the ICON and Acute Optic Neuritis Network (ACON) criteria for CRMP5-IgG+ON, using patients with late-onset (age ≥50 years) aquaporin-4-IgG-positive (AQP4-IgG+)-ON or myelin-oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody (MOG-IgG+)-ON for comparison. We developed the "CRMP score," based on typical CRMP5-IgG+ON clinical features, to guide CRMP5 antibody testing in ON.The study included 17 patients with CRMP5-IgG+, 11 with AQP4-IgG+ON, and 13 with MOG-IgG+ON. Application of ICON criteria yielded no "definite ON" and 1 "probable ON" diagnosis among the 17 CRMP5-IgG+ cases, but definite ON diagnoses for 6 of 11 AQP4-IgG+ (55%, p = 0.003) and 7 of 13 MOG-IgG+ cases (54%, p = 0.001). ACON criteria yielded definite ON diagnoses for 2 (12%) CRMP5-IgG+ON, 10 (91%) of the AQP4-IgG+ON, and 13 (100%) of the MOG-IgG+ON (p < 0.001). A CRMP score ≥1 identified CRMP5-IgG+ON with a sensitivity of 88.2% and a specificity of 87.5%.ICON and ACON criteria for ON diagnosis identified only a minority of CRMP5-IgG+ON cases; thus, we developed the "CRMP" score to aid their identification in clinical practice.

title: End-to-end film-based characterization of gated delivery latencies in a spot-scanned synchrotron-based proton therapy system.
abstract: Temporal mismatches between gating signals and beam activation-beam-on and beam-off latencies-in gated particle beam therapy can compromise dose integrity. Yet standardized measurement techniques are lacking, and system-specific characterization, particularly for synchrotron-based proton systems, remains limited.To implement a novel strategy for precise end-to-end gating latency measurements of a spot-scanned proton beam using Gafchromic film.Gating latencies have been measured for a Hitachi ProBeat accelerator equipped with a Varian RPM gating system. EBT4 films were positioned within a stack of acrylic blocks on a QUASAR respiratory motion platform operated with a 1.5 cm amplitude and 12 bpm sinusoidal pattern. A stainless-steel ball bearing (BB), positioned atop the film, facilitated localization. During irradiation, the BB produced a dose shadow on the film that indicated the phantom position. A proton plan consisting of a single 85.3 MeV spot was delivered to isocenter during a single gate-on/off interval initiated near the 25% phase, to maximize phantom velocity. Fifty-one measurements were made with a variety of gating intervals. Beam-on latency and delivery time produced a separation between the BB-shadow and the centroid of the Gaussian proton spot. Spot duration information was extracted from accelerator log files. BB-shadow/spot separation is modeled analytically based on phantom motion enabling the direct calculation of the total beam-on and beam-off latencies. Accelerator latency was measured directly with an oscilloscope, enabling isolation of the relative contributions of the RPM gating system.An average beam-on latency of 142 ± 27  ms is observed for the RPM+ProBeat system for the first gate of a delivery, which includes a known 69 ms beam extraction judgment time for the first proton spot in a spill from the Hitachi synchrotron. The corresponding average beam-off latency is 87 ± 30  ms  . The average gate-on and gate-off latencies of the RPM system are calculated as 72 ± 27  ms  and 81 ± 30  ms  , respectively. The associated average contributions of the accelerator to the beam-on latencies are measured as 69.3 ± 0.2  ms  (first gate in new spill) and 0.53 ± 0.07  ms  (subsequent gates in existing spill) and similarly 6 ± 4  ms  for beam-off latency.A novel, high-precision method for gating-latency measurements has been implemented using film to characterize gating latencies in a spot-scanned particle beam. Commissioning and regular quality assurance methods to precisely characterize the temporal accuracy of a gating system ensure treatment accuracy and will become increasingly vital to consider for higher-frequency applications, such as cardiac gating or FLASH-capable systems.© 2026 The Author(s). title: Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement: Clinical Challenges, Evolving Indications, and Future Directions.
abstract: Mitral regurgitation is a highly prevalent valvular heart disease and, when hemodynamically significant, is associated with adverse outcomes. Despite advances in surgical techniques and catheter-based edge-to-edge repair, a large number of patients remain untreated due to high surgical risk or anatomical limitations. Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) has emerged as a promising therapeutic option for these patients. Over the past 15 years, the TMVR field has substantially progressed, with multiple devices advancing to human clinical evaluation. This review aims to provide an overview of the key milestones in TMVR development, patient selection pathways, and the transition from transapical to transseptal delivery. We further summarize the available clinical outcomes across different platforms and discuss remaining knowledge gaps, as well as future directions for this evolving field.© 2026 The Author(s).

title: Fingerprinting the polycystic kidney: radiomics of the noncystic parenchyma for earlier ADPKD detection.
abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease risk stratification relies on total kidney volume, a validated marker of cyst burden and progression. Kremer et al.'s pilot study used rapid breath-hold magnetic resonance fingerprinting with radiomics to evaluate noncystic renal parenchyma in children and young adults. Quantitative T1/T2 texture features distinguished autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease from controls independently of total kidney volume, cyst fraction, age, or body size, suggesting early tissue changes. llm_summary: Researchers used a magnetic resonance imaging technique to examine whether changes in kidney tissue itself, not just cyst size, could help detect autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease earlier in children and young adults. They found that texture patterns in the healthy kidney tissue could distinguish patients with the disease from healthy controls, independent of cyst burden or body size, suggesting tissue damage occurs before visible cysts form. title: Weakly supervised deep learning distinguishes alcohol-associated from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis on H&E whole-slide images.
abstract: Distinguishing alcohol-associated steatohepatitis (ASH) from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is challenging given the absence of pathognomonic differentiators. We developed and evaluated a weakly supervised deep learning model, as a single-institution proof-of-concept study, to test whether routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images (WSIs) of liver biopsies contain sufficient morphological information to predict steatohepatitis etiology at the slide level. A retrospective cohort of 1147 WSIs was assembled (train set: 1007, holdout test set: 140). Models were trained using 5-fold patient-level cross-validation at ×20 and ×40 magnification. Model interpretability was assessed through attention-based clustering with blinded pathologist review of high-attention patches. The ×20 model achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic of 0.86 ± 0.01 on the test set, with balanced accuracy of 0.80. The ×40 model performed comparably. Specificity was high (0.93 at ×20), with an ASH sensitivity of 0.67 at ×20. Fibrosis-stratified showed preserved performance at advanced fibrosis (stage ≥3) with balanced accuracy of 82.5% and ASH sensitivity of 77.4%. Attention-based clustering localized ASH-enriched regions to active injury patterns including Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophilic inflammation, cholestatic change, and pericellular fibrosis, whereas MASH-enriched regions showed steatosis with lower inflammatory activity. Weakly supervised deep learning applied to routine liver H&E WSIs can discriminate ASH from MASH with performance preserved at advanced fibrosis. The comparable performance of ×20 and ×40 magnification, and the alignment of model attention with established histological features, support the use of routine morphology as a decision-support input in cases with incomplete or conflicting clinical histories, particularly when the etiological distinction has the greatest implications for management.© 2026 The Author(s).

title: Survival benefit of chemoradiotherapy in limited-stage mantle cell lymphoma: a National Cancer Database analysis.
abstract: Limited-stage mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) is rare, and optimal management remains undefined because of limited representation in clinical studies. We conducted a large population-based analysis using the National Cancer Database to evaluate overall survival (OS) in patients with Ann Arbor stage I to II MCL diagnosed between 2004 and 2015. Initial treatment was categorized to chemotherapy alone, radiotherapy (RT) alone, or combined chemotherapy plus RT (Chemo+RT), and outcomes were further stratified by stage and era of diagnosis (2004-2009 vs 2010-2015) to account for advances in systemic therapy, such as the adoption of bendamustine-rituximab for frontline therapy and the availability of Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors for relapsed disease. Among 2428 patients included, median OS for the entire cohort was 8.1 years. Chemo+RT was associated with superior OS compared with chemotherapy alone or RT alone (median OS, 11.2 vs 7.4 vs 8.0 years, respectively; P < .001). This survival benefit was observed in both stage I and stage II diseases and in both eras. On multivariable analysis, treatment with chemotherapy alone (hazard ratio [HR], 1.50) or RT alone (HR, 1.33) was independently associated with inferior OS compared with Chemo+RT. In this, to our knowledge, largest real-world analysis of limited-stage MCL to date, combined chemoimmunotherapy and RT was associated with a clinically meaningful survival benefit, including in the modern treatment era. title: Reliability of computational versus noncomputational metrics of working memory and episodic memory in serious mental illness.
abstract: Computational models can be used to decompose overall behavior into individual parameters that are designed to isolate specific cognitive and neural processes and provide new information about psychiatric disorders. However, it is not yet clear whether these computational parameters have sufficient reliability to replace traditional noncomputational metrics, especially in severe mental illness. The present study asked whether computational parameters can be as reliable as, or even more reliable than, noncomputational performance metrics in healthy control participants (n = 105) and people with schizophrenia spectrum disorder (n = 72), bipolar disorder (n = 68), and major depressive disorder (n = 76). These participants were tested in working memory and episodic memory paradigms. We applied a computational model that yielded parameters corresponding to memory storage capacity, memory precision, and the rate of attention lapses. We also examined a noncomputational metric of performance, the mean error. Each participant was tested twice, separated by at least 28 days. In most cases, the computational parameters exhibited good-to-excellent split-half and test-retest reliability (>0.80) that was comparable with the reliability of the noncomputational performance metric. In one case, reliability was substantially better for the memory precision parameter than for the noncomputational metric. In another case, reliability for the memory precision parameter was substantially lower but was improved by the use of hierarchical Bayesian estimation. Thus, when applied thoughtfully, parameters derived from computational models can have excellent psychometric properties, providing a reliable means of isolating the factors that underlie individual and group differences in studies of mental illness. title: Approximately 30% of Patients Undergoing Knee Cartilage Biopsy Subsequently Undergo Matrix-Induced Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation at a Mean 4.3-Year Follow-Up.
abstract: To evaluate implantation rates, time to implantation, and predictors of implantation following matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation (MACI) biopsy for knee chondral defects.Patients undergoing MACI biopsy or implantation for symptomatic knee chondral defects from 2017 to 2024 at a single institution were reviewed. At a minimum 1-year follow-up, the decision to proceed with implantation, recurrent symptoms, complications, and reoperations were assessed. Kaplan-Meier analysis estimated time to implantation, and multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of MACI implantation.A total of 208 knees in 202 patients (mean age 28.0 ± 10.9 years, range 11-59) underwent MACI biopsy for 243 chondral defects (patella [38%], femoral condyle [34%], and trochlea [26%]). At a mean follow-up of 4.3 years (range 1.0-8.3), 64 knees (31%) proceeded to second-stage MACI implantation. Among 144 knees not implanted, 87 (60%) reported symptom improvement, and 26 (18%) had persistent symptoms. The remaining 22% did not undergo implantation due to another cartilage procedure, insurance denial, or pending scheduling. Patients who underwent biopsy at the home institution had a shorter time from biopsy to implantation compared with those biopsied at outside institutions (6.1 vs 13.1 months, P = .001). Median time to implantation was 9.4 months (95% confidence level: 7.2-12.2) for home biopsies. Lower body mass index was associated with progression to implantation after adjusting for covariates (odds ratios 0.92, P = .019). Patients implanted within 4 months had larger chondral defects (4.0 vs 3.0 cm2, P = .045). At a mean 4.1-year follow-up, 6 patients (8%) experienced postoperative complications, including 3 (4%) who required revision chondroplasty.MACI biopsy for knee chondral defects resulted in approximately one-third of patients proceeding to MACI implantation, at a median of 9.4 months after biopsy. Lower body mass index was associated with higher likelihood of progression to implantation, larger chondral defects with earlier implantation, and among patients who did not proceed to implantation, approximately 60% reported symptom improvement following concomitant chondroplasty at the time of biopsy.Level IV, retrospective case series.© 2026 the Arthroscopy Association of North America.

title: Reduced Phrenic CMAP Amplitudes in Obesity Despite Preserved Diaphragm Ultrasound Measures.
abstract: Phrenic nerve conduction studies (NCS) are regularly used in the evaluation of neuromuscular respiratory dysfunction; however, the impact of body mass index (BMI) on phrenic compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes remains poorly characterized. We evaluated the relationship between BMI and phrenic CMAP amplitudes in patients without evidence of neuromuscular diaphragmatic dysfunction.We performed a retrospective secondary analysis of patients derived from two previously published cohorts from Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota) and the University of Alberta (Edmonton, Alberta) evaluating diaphragm ultrasound in suspected neuromuscular respiratory insufficiency. Patients without evidence of neuromuscular disease affecting the diaphragm who underwent bilateral phrenic NCS and diaphragm ultrasound were included.Seventy-nine patients met inclusion criteria, including 36 with BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2. Median phrenic CMAP amplitudes were significantly lower in patients with BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 compared to BMI < 30 kg/m2 (0.25 mV [IQR 0.10-0.38] vs. 0.50 mV [0.30-0.65], p < 0.001). Low phrenic CMAP amplitudes (< 0.3 mV) were more common in patients with obesity (58% vs. 21%, p < 0.001). BMI demonstrated a moderate negative correlation with phrenic CMAP amplitude (ρ = -0.50, p < 0.001). Diaphragm thickness at functional residual capacity did not differ significantly between BMI groups, while diaphragm thickening ratio was modestly lower in obesity.Elevated BMI is associated with lower phrenic CMAP amplitudes in patients without evidence of neuromuscular diaphragmatic dysfunction. Reduced phrenic CMAP amplitudes in obesity may reflect technical recording limitations rather than clinically meaningful diaphragmatic dysfunction. Low-amplitude phrenic responses in patients with obesity should be interpreted cautiously and alongside adjunctive assessments such as diaphragm ultrasound.© 2026 The Author(s). title: The radiographic effect of cage subsidence on neuroforamina after anterior cervical discectomy and fusion.
abstract: Retrospective Cohort Study.The objective of this study is to investigate the effect of cage subsidence on neuroforaminal area after anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) utilizing computed tomography (CT).Restoration of disc height via implantation of an interbody device provides an indirect decompression of the cervical neuroforamina. Interbody cage subsidence is a potential postoperative occurrence, but the effect of this on neuroforaminal area has yet to be characterized.A retrospective review was conducted of patients who underwent one- to four-levels of ACDF utilizing an interbody device with anterior plating. Cage subsidence, neuroforaminal area, height and width were measured on CT scans preoperatively and at least 6 months postoperatively. Levels with a cumulative sum of cranial and caudal subsidence greater than 4 mm were classified as severely subsided, while levels with cumulative subsidence less than 4 mm were classified as non-severely subsided.A total of 83 patients (151 levels) were included in this retrospective analysis. Average endplate subsidence was 3.2 ± 1.9 mm. Non-severely subsided levels demonstrated a greater perioperative increase in neuroforaminal area (7.9 vs 2.1 mm2, p < 0.001), neuroforaminal height (1.1 vs 0.4 mm, p < 0.001) and neuroforaminal width (0.7 vs 0.1 mm, p < 0.001) compared to severely subsided levels. Interbody subsidence significantly predicted a decreased change in neuroforaminal height, width and area (p < 0.001). Severe subsidence was associated with an increased rate of pseudarthrosis, but similar reoperation rates and recurrent neurologic deficits between the two groups.Severe subsidence of interbody cages after an ACDF was associated with a decreased perioperative change in neuroforaminal dimensions. This decrease in the size of the neuroforamen may reduce the effect of indirect decompression of the nerve root.Published by Elsevier Ltd.
