llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a protein called Nrf2, which helps cells manage stress, is necessary for blood vessels in muscles to adapt to exercise training. Exercise training improved blood vessel function in normal rats but not in rats lacking Nrf2, suggesting this protein is important for some exercise-related adaptations. However, other pathways independent of Nrf2 can still maintain blood vessel function and respond to exercise training.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers examined vascular responses of resistance arterioles from the soleus muscle in wild-type and Nrf2 knockout rats following exercise training or cage confinement to determine whether the redox-sensitive transcription factor Nrf2 is necessary for exercise-induced vascular adaptations. Exercise training enhanced flow-induced vasodilation in arterioles from wild-type rats but not in arterioles from Nrf2 knockout rats, and myogenic responses were greater in trained wild-type arterioles compared to trained Nrf2 knockout arterioles. Both wild-type and Nrf2 knockout arterioles showed enhanced vasodilation to the nitric oxide donor DEA-NONO-ate and increased contractile responses to phenylephrine following exercise training. Expression of calcium-activated potassium channels was reduced in arterioles from Nrf2 knockout rats compared to wild-type rats. Although Nrf2 appears necessary for flow-induced vasodilation and myogenic adaptations to exercise training in skeletal muscle arterioles, Nrf2-independent compensatory pathways maintain and can be upregulated by exercise.

title: Efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and stage 2-3 fibrosis: a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled study.
abstract: Efinopegdutide is a pharmacologically distinct once-weekly GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist with a relative receptor potency balance of approximately 2:1 under development for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). We aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with non-cirrhotic MASH.We did a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind study conducted at 176 academic and community centres in 26 countries. We included adults (aged ≥18 years) with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage 2 or stage 3 fibrosis. Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1:1) to receive either efinopegdutide (4 mg, 7 mg, or 10 mg), placebo, or open-label semaglutide 2·4 mg, all administered subcutaneously once weekly. Randomisation was performed centrally. The primary endpoint was MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis at week 52. The key secondary histological endpoint was fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis. Missing end-of-treatment biopsies were considered as failure for the primary analysis. This study is registered with EU CT, 2022-502647-35-00, and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05877547, and is complete.Between June 23, 2023, and Dec 29, 2025, we screened 1704 participants. We randomly assigned 386 (23%) participants, of whom 381 (99%; 194 [51%] women and 187 [49%] men) received at least one dose of study intervention and were included in the analysis. Baseline characteristics were similar across groups; 239 (63%) of 381 participants had F2 fibrosis and 142 (37%) had F3 fibrosis; the mean age of participants was 53 years (SD 13). At week 52, MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 31 (56%) of 55 participants in the 4 mg efinopegdutide group, 31 (63%) of 49 participants in the 7 mg efinopegdutide group, and 35 (61%) of 57 participants in the 10 mg efinopegdutide group versus seven (13%) of 53 participants in the placebo group (difference vs placebo 43·0 percentage points [95% CI 25·7 to 57·8; p<0·0001] for 4 mg, 49·5 percentage points [31·4 to 64·2; p<0·0001] for 7 mg, and 47·8 percentage points [30·7 to 62·0; p<0·0001] for 10 mg); 26 (53%) of 49 participants receiving semaglutide met this endpoint. For the key secondary endpoint, fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis occurred in 32 (43%) of 75 participants in the efinopegdutide 4 mg group, 39 (52%) of 75 participants in the 7 mg efinopegdutide group, and 26 (34%) of 77 participants in the efinopegdutide 10 mg group versus 16 (21%) of 77 participants receiving placebo (difference vs placebo 21·7 percentage points [7·1 to 35·7; p=0·0038] in the efinopegdutide 4 mg group, 30·4 percentage points [15·4 to 44·3; p<0·0001] in the efinopegdutide 7 mg group, and 13·0 percentage points [-1·2 to 26·8; p=0·072] in the efinopegdutide 10 mg group); 16 (25%) of 65 participants receiving semaglutide met this endpoint. The most frequently reported adverse events with efinopegdutide were gastrointestinal, with the highest rates among participants receiving efinopegdutide 10 mg. Adverse events leading to discontinuation of study intervention occurred more frequently among participants receiving efinopegdutide 10 mg (nine [11%] of 79 participants) compared with the other doses of efinopegdutide (range 3-4%) or placebo (one [1%]).Treatment with efinopegdutide resulted in a significantly greater proportion of participants with MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis compared with placebo. The 7 mg dose showed the most favourable benefit-risk profile, improving fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening steatohepatitis in approximately half of participants after 1 year of treatment. These findings support the potential utility of efinopegdutide as a once-weekly GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist in MASH.Merck Sharp & Dohme, a subsidiary of Merck & Co.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. llm_summary: Researchers tested a new weekly injection called efinopegdutide in adults with a liver disease involving fat buildup and scarring to see if it could improve their condition. After one year, about 56-63% of patients receiving efinopegdutide showed improvement compared to only 13% receiving placebo, with the 7 mg dose appearing safest and most effective. The most common side effects were digestive problems, though the findings suggest this treatment could help people with this liver disease.
llm_summary_expert: This phase 2b randomized controlled trial evaluated efinopegdutide, a GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist administered once weekly at doses of 4 mg, 7 mg, or 10 mg, compared with placebo and open-label semaglutide 2.4 mg in 381 adults with biopsy-confirmed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and stage 2-3 fibrosis. The primary endpoint was MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis at week 52, and the key secondary endpoint was fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis. At week 52, MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 56-63% of participants receiving efinopegdutide across all three doses compared with 13% in the placebo group (p<0.0001 for all doses), while fibrosis improvement without worsening steatohepatitis occurred in 43-52% of efinopegdutide recipients versus 21% receiving.

title: Superficial Ewing Sarcoma and Neurocristic FET::ETS Tumors: Defining a Diagnostic Gray Zone.
abstract: Superficial small round cell tumors harboring FET::ETS fusions and expressing S100 and/or SOX10 present a diagnostic challenge, as they raise consideration of both Ewing sarcoma and superficial neurocristic tumor (SNT), with distinct clinical implications. We performed clinicopathologic, immunohistochemical, and DNA methylation analysis on 14 superficial small round cell tumors with S100, variable SOX10 expression, and FET::ETS fusions (n=12) or EWSR1 rearrangements (n=2). The cohort included 9 females and 5 males (age 10-70 years). Tumors were classified as SNT (n=2) based on the presence of morphologic features reported in the initial descriptions: (1) superficial location, (2) nests or cords of bland round to ovoid cells, (3) lack of necrosis, and (4) diffuse co-expression of S100 and SOX10. Cases of Ewing sarcoma (n=8) were composed of nests or sheets of primitive round cells with malignant cytology regardless of S100/SOX10 status, while cases with some but not all features of SNT were labeled "Difficult to classify" (n=4). Clustering by DNA methylome was concordant with histologic classification in 9 of 10 confidently classified tumors and consistently classified all SOX10-expressing tumors as SNT regardless of morphology, including the "Difficult to classify" cases. Differential methylation analysis demonstrated hypomethylation of neural crest-related genes in SNT. Copy number variation was significantly higher in the Ewing sarcoma methylation cluster, with recurrent chromosome 8 gains, whereas tumors in the SNT cluster were largely copy number neutral. Despite clustering with SNT by DNA methylation profiling, two of the "Difficult to classify" cases showed at least focal high-grade cytology and had distant metastases, including one dying of disease. Pooled survival analysis of published and current cases demonstrated superior outcome of SNT when compared to all Ewing sarcomas, but no significant differences in overall survival comparing SNT to superficial Ewing sarcoma. Our findings support a cautious diagnostic approach, reserving the diagnosis of SNT for tumors with classic morphologic and immunophenotypic features, while regarding cytologically high-grade or ambiguous lesions as representing Ewing sarcoma for clinical purposes, until the precise nosology of these exceptionally rare tumors is better understood.Copyright © 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined 14 superficial tumors with genetic fusions to determine whether they should be classified as Ewing sarcoma or a rarer neurocristic tumor, since this distinction affects treatment decisions. DNA analysis showed that tumors with classic features and specific protein markers clustered together as neurocristic tumors and had better survival outcomes than Ewing sarcoma. The study recommends diagnosing tumors with ambiguous features as Ewing sarcoma until these exceptionally rare tumors are better understood.

Tumors were classified as superficial neurocristic tumor (n=2) when displaying superficial location, nests or cords of bland cells, absent necrosis, and diffuse S100/SOX10 co-expression, whereas Ewing sarcoma (n=8) showed nests or sheets of primitive cells with malignant cytology, with four cases designated "Difficult to classify" based on intermediate features. title: Clinical Consensus Guidelines on Antibiotic Prescribing Practices for Infants with Gastroschisis Utilizing Modified Delphi Methodology.
abstract: Gastroschisis is the most common congenital abdominal wall defect in newborns and common surgical diagnosis for which antibiotics are prescribed in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). Multiple studies demonstrate early and prolonged antibiotic exposure, despite evidence of overuse resulting in delayed initiation of feedings, later full feedings, and blood stream infection. The purpose was to develop expert consensus on evidence-driven clinical guidelines for microbiologic screening and antibiotic usage in neonates with simple gastroschisis.The Children's Hospitals Neonatal Consortium (CHNC) Gastroschisis Focus Group utilized a modified Delphi method to develop clinical consensus guidelines (CCG). Committee leaders drafted 10 recommendations after literature review and group discussion. Each recommendation was sent to focus group members via REDCap survey tool and members scored responses on a 5-point Likert scale.In the first survey, there were 23 respondents and 7/10 recommendations received a mean score >80%, meeting the criteria for consensus. Following review of results and comments, the remaining statements were edited and sent out for the second round survey where all achieved consensus. Themes included the practice of screening for infection at birth by blood culture, and antibiotic use practices at the time of birth and abdominal wall closure. These included risk stratification for infection, spectrum of antibiotic therapies utilized, length of therapy, and timing of antibiotic administration.We present a consensus evidence-based framework for antibiotic use and stewardship practices in infants with simple gastroschisis, which will be important as many centers lack standardized guidelines in this population.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Researchers used expert surveys to develop standardized guidelines for antibiotic use in newborns with gastroschisis, a common birth defect of the abdominal wall. After two rounds of voting, the expert panel reached agreement on recommendations covering when to screen for infection, which antibiotics to use, and how long to treat patients. These new guidelines aim to reduce unnecessary antibiotic exposure and improve outcomes for affected infants.
llm_summary_expert: The Children's Hospitals Neonatal Consortium Gastroschisis Focus Group used a modified Delphi methodology to develop evidence-based clinical consensus guidelines for antibiotic prescribing and microbiologic screening in neonates with simple gastroschisis. In the first survey round, 23 respondents evaluated 10 recommendations on a 5-point Likert scale, with 7 of 10 recommendations achieving consensus defined as a mean score greater than 80%. Following review and revision of the remaining three recommendations, all 10 statements achieved consensus in the second survey round. The final guidelines addressed risk stratification for infection, antibiotic spectrum selection, duration of therapy, and timing of administration at birth and abdominal wall closure. These consensus recommendations provide a standardized framework for antibiotic stewardship in infants with simple gastroschisis, addressing a gap in clinical practice guidelines across many centers.

title: Can Outpatient Total Knee Arthroplasty Be Performed at a Complex, Academic, Quaternary Referral Center?
abstract: Outpatient (same-day discharge) primary total knee arthroplasties (TKAs) have been recently popularized, but results from academic medical centers remain limited. Outpatient surgery shifts perioperative responsibilities to the surgeon. Meanwhile, surgeon reimbursements continue to decrease. We retrospectively evaluated 90-day rates of emergency room (ER) visits, reoperations, revisions, and incoming/outgoing postoperative patient touches associated with outpatient TKAs at our complex, academic, quaternary referral center.At our institution, 1,787 outpatient primary TKAs were performed between 2019 and 2024 in 1,552 unique patients. The mean age was 65 years, 51% were women, the mean body mass index (BMI) was 33, the mean American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) score was 2.4, and the mean Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) was 1.5 (range, 0 to 10). Medical comorbidities, ER visits, reoperations, revisions, and postoperative touches within 90 days after TKA were collected. Univariate logistic regression analyses were completed.The rates of ER visits, reoperations, and revisions within 90 days of surgery were 8.5, 3.1, and 0.7%, respectively. Knees averaged nine postoperative touches, and total touches increased from 61 in 2019 to greater than 5,800 in 2024. The most common first-time ER visit reason was a medical issue unrelated to surgery (35%), followed by evaluation for venous thromboembolism (VTE; 29%). The actual VTE incidence was 0.6%. The most common reoperation was manipulation under anesthesia (MUA; incidence 1.5%). The 90-day periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) incidence was 0.7%, and all cases required reoperation or revision. Older age and increasing ASA score were significantly associated with risk of ER visits (odds ratio [OR] 1.2; P = 0.01 and OR 1.8; P < 0.001, respectively). Increasing CCI was significantly associated with risk of ER visits (OR 1.2; P = 0.001), revisions (OR 1.5; P = 0.001), and PJI (OR 1.3; P = 0.02).We found a high rate of ER visits within 90 days after outpatient TKAs, with nearly 40% unattributable to surgery. Increasing age and comorbidities were associated with increased ER visit risk, and comorbidities also increased revision and PJI risk. Knees averaged nine non-clinic postoperative touches.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether knee replacement surgery could be safely performed as outpatient procedures at a major academic medical center, tracking complications within 90 days for nearly 1,800 surgeries. About 8.5% of patients visited the emergency room after surgery, though more than one-third of these visits were for medical issues unrelated to the surgery itself. Patients with more existing health conditions faced higher risks of emergency visits and complications, suggesting that outpatient knee replacement may work best for healthier individuals.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers retrospectively evaluated 1,787 outpatient primary total knee arthroplasties performed at an academic quaternary referral center between 2019 and 2024 in 1,552 patients with mean age 65 years, mean BMI 33, and mean ASA score 2.4, assessing 90-day rates of emergency room visits, reoperations, revisions, and postoperative patient touches. The study found 90-day rates of 8.5% for emergency room visits, 3.1% for reoperations, and 0.7% for revisions, with periprosthetic joint infection incidence of 0.7% and manipulation under anesthesia incidence of 1.5%. Older age and higher ASA scores were significantly associated with increased risk of emergency room visits, while increasing Charlson Comorbidity Index was significantly associated with increased risk of emergency room visits, revisions, and periprosthetic joint infection. The most common reason for first-time emergency room visits was a medical issue unrelated to surgery (35%), followed by evaluation for venous thromboembol.

title: Prevalence and Consequences of Guideline-Directed Indications for Aortic Valve Replacement in the EARLY TAVR Trial.
abstract: The current American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association valvular heart disease guidelines were published before several recent trials that provide greater support for early intervention in patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (AS).This study sought to investigate the prevalence and clinical impact of American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Class II recommendations for AVR in the EARLY TAVR trial.The EARLY TAVR trial randomized patients with asymptomatic severe AS to transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance (CS) with conversion to TAVR based on development of ACC/AHA Class I indications. Patients in the intention-to-treat cohort were stratified by presence of a Class II indication for AVR at randomization. The primary endpoint of the present analysis was the composite of all-cause death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization. Interaction tests were performed to assess whether the treatment effect differed by level of guideline recommendation. Timing of conversion to AVR in the CS group according to the presence/absence of Class II indications was also assessed.Of the 901 patients randomized to TAVR (N = 445) and CS (N = 446), 636 (70.6%) patients had no guideline recommendation, and 265 (29.4%) had at least1 1 Class II recommendation for AVR at the time of randomization. At a median follow-up of 3.8 years, patients with a Class II indication for AVR experienced higher rates of the primary endpoint (Class II: 24.5% vs no recommendation: 14.5%; HR = 1.78; 95% CI: 1.30-2.44; P < 0.001) and were more likely to have acute valve syndrome at the time of conversion. Compared with CS, the relative benefit of early TAVR on the primary endpoint was similar regardless of the presence or absence of a Class II guideline recommendation (HR = 0.62; 95% CI: 0.37-1.02 vs 0.61; 95% CI: 0.40-0.92; Pinteraction = 0.96).Among patients in the EARLY TAVR trial, Class II indications for AVR were present in almost one-third of patients at baseline. The benefit of early TAVR was consistent regardless of the presence or absence of Class II indications. These findings support the strategy of early TAVR over CS in asymptomatic patients with severe AS, independent of guideline indications.https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03042104; Unique Identifier: NCT03042104.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether early valve replacement surgery benefited patients with severe aortic stenosis (a narrowing of the heart valve) who had no symptoms, comparing those who received immediate treatment to those who waited for symptoms to develop. Nearly one-third of patients showed warning signs at the start of the study, and these patients had worse outcomes overall, but early treatment reduced serious complications equally well regardless of whether warning signs were present. The findings suggest that offering early valve replacement to asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis may improve their health outcomes.

The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization, with median follow-up of 3.8 years. title: Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry-Derived Body Composition Asymmetry in Pain-Free Adults: Associations With Age, Lumbar Disc Degeneration, and Physical Activity.
abstract: To characterize body composition asymmetry in asymptomatic adults and examine its associations with age, lumbar intervertebral disc degeneration (DD), and physical activity.Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scans were performed, and lumbar DD grading, and physical activity levels were assessed in clinically asymptomatic adults in this cross-sectional study.Fifty-one participants were included. Asymmetry in trunk fat and lean tissue mass was present in the overall cohort (P<0.0001), and leg lean tissue mass also differed between sides (P=0.0178), with right-sided predominance in older participants (P=0.0094). Trunk lean AI (TLAI) was higher in older than younger participants (6.3±4.9 vs. 3.5±2.6; P=0.012), whereas the corresponding trunk fat AI (TFAI) difference was not statistically significant (8.0±5.9 vs. 5.0±3.6; P=0.085). Greater age was associated with TLAI (P=0.008), while the trunk fat association was less robust in sensitivity analyses. Signed TFAI and TLAI shifted toward non-dominant-side predominance with greater age (P<0.05). Lumbar DD and physical activity were not significantly associated with asymmetry.Body composition asymmetry was most evident in the trunk. Trunk lean asymmetry was greater at older ages, whereas the corresponding trunk fat association was weaker. Because functional outcomes were not assessed, the clinical significance of these findings requires further investigation.Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. All rights reserved.

They found that asymmetry was most noticeable in the trunk, with older adults showing greater muscle imbalance between sides compared to younger adults, while spine degeneration and physical activity showed no significant association with asymmetry. The clinical importance of these findings remains unclear because the study did not measure whether asymmetry affects how people function or move.

title: Evaluating Age-Related Motor System Changes Using Gait as a Functionally Relevant Marker.
abstract: Aging causes gait and mobility decline, which often precedes cognitive impairment and dementia. Biological "age gaps" (the difference between biological and chronological age) are traditionally measured using neuroimaging and electroencephalography, quantified gait metrics have not been used for this purpose. We hypothesize that specific gait metrics can effectively quantify biological aging and predict future cognitive impairment risk.We analyzed gait data from the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, a population-based cohort in Olmsted County, MN. Participants without known gait disorder, recruited between 2007 and 2025, were included. We used these data to develop a machine learning-based age prediction model. This gait-based age prediction model was used to devise the "gait age gap," a quantified metric of gait abnormality defined as the difference between age as predicted by gait performance ("gait age") and chronological age. We used the gait age gap to evaluate the risk of future cognitive impairment.We analyzed 19,637 walk trials from 5,794 unique participants (49% female), with a mean age of 78 (±8) years. Gait age was primarily driven by changes in measures of stability. A larger gait age gap was associated with impaired cognitive and functional status. In longitudinal analysis, each gait age gap year exceeding chronological age increased the risk of converting from a normal to cognitively impaired (CI) state by 7% per year. Gait age gap outperformed baseline velocity in distinguishing normal from CI groups and was associated with future risk of conversion from normal to a CI state hazard ratio = 1.07 (95% CI 1.03-1.13) for gait age gap vs hazard ratio = 0.99 (95% CI 0.98-1.00) for velocity.The gait age gap is a functionally relevant marker of age-related motor system changes that quantifies deviations from expected gait performance for a given chronological age. It is associated with a higher risk of future cognitive impairment among cognitively normal individuals. This study includes a relatively homogeneous cohort of predominantly Caucasian participants. To assess generalizability and the trajectory of motoric aging across sociodemographic groups, these findings need to be replicated in diverse cohorts. Wearable sensor technologies could also make such measures more scalable.

title: Next-Gen Bipolar RF for Skin Tightening and Predictive Results: First Clinical Evaluation of the Quantum probe in Body Contouring.
abstract: Radiofrequency (RF) devices have gained prominence as a minimally invasive technique to improve skin tightening and aesthetic outcomes following liposculpture. However, existing technologies present limitations in treatment precision and safety.To assess skin retraction outcomes and complication rates following Quantum RF treatment in patients undergoing High-Definition Liposculpture (HDL).We conducted a prospective cohort study in a single plastic surgery center in Bogotá, Colombia, from February to September 2024. Thirty-one consecutive patients undergoing HDL were treated with Quantum RF across one or more body areas. Skin elasticity was objectively measured using a dynamometer on the different body areas pre- and post-procedure. Bivariate subgroup analysis was performed by anatomical region, age group, and Fitzpatrick phototype.A total of 31 consecutive patients were analyzed. Cohort was predominantly female (90.3%) and Hispanic (83.9%), mean age of 39.5 years (SD 8.22). Mean body mass index (BMI) was 23.3 kg/m2 (SD 2.76). Mean percentage improvement in abdominal skin elasticity was 20.1% (SD 5.77%), with treated areas showing significantly greater improvements compared to non-treated contralateral controls (6.8%, p < 0.001). Across anatomical regions, mean skin retraction was 21.5% for the abdomen, 18.7% for arms, 19.3% for back, and 16.9% for thighs. The most pronounced improvement was observed in patients aged 26-30 with phototype IV, reaching up to 40% elasticity gain. The overall complication rate was 13%, with only 6.5% representing minor thermal injuries near access sites.Preliminary findings suggest that the Quantum RF probe is a safe and effective modality for subdermal tissue tightening in HDL, with consistent improvements in skin elasticity across multiple regions and skin phototypes. title: Intra-articular knee injections in adults aged 40 to 60 years and the likelihood of progression to joint arthroplasty.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and disability in adults. Intra-articular injections are important components in the management of knee OA symptoms, but there are concerns that these injections may be associated with the progression of OA. Therefore, this study determined how the likelihood of progression to arthroplasty is influenced by intra-articular injection of corticosteroid (CS) and/or hyaluronic acid (HA) in patients with knee OA.This population-based cohort study included patients aged 40 to 60 years receiving an initial intra-articular injection of CS and/or HA from 1 January 2000 through 31 December 2010, who resided in Olmsted County, Minnesota, USA. The primary outcome was the likelihood of joint arthroplasty by number of intra-articular injections received evaluated by Cox proportional hazards regression.A total of 1,897 patients (n = 2,336 knees) who received 8,600 injections (n = 5,786 CS; n = 2,814 HA) were included (mean age 51.9 years (SD 5.5); 1,515 females (64.9%); mean BMI 34.8 kg/m2 (SD 8.0)), and 917 (39.3%) subsequently underwent arthroplasty. Accounting for age, BMI, and Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grade at initial injection, the number of intra-articular injections was associated with an increased likelihood of arthroplasty (hazard ratio (HR) 1.12 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.17)). For patients with early OA (KL grade 0 to 1), CS injections (HR 1.27 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.37)) were associated with an increased likelihood of arthroplasty versus HA (HR 1.12 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.19)).Each intra-articular injection was associated with a 12% increased likelihood of arthroplasty. title: Validation of an LC-Q-TOF "HiRes Mass-fix" assay for improved sensitivity and specificity of M-protein detection.
abstract: To validate a blood-based liquid chromatography quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MS) method "HiRes Mass-Fix" as a fit-for-purpose, patient-specific method for detecting low level M-proteins in patients who have reached negativity by MALDI-TOF MS "Mass-Fix".Analytical validation included precision, accuracy, analytical measurement interval, limit of detection, specificity, ion suppression, carryover, and extracted-sample stability. Clinical performance was assessed by comparing 174 patients with bone marrow (BM) measurable residual disease (MRD) by next-generation flow cytometry (NGF) to both Mass-Fix and HiRes Mass-Fix.HiRes Mass-Fix demonstrated acceptable precision, accuracy, linearity, specificity, and stability for its intended use, with an average limit of detection of 3.8 mg/L. HiRes Mass-Fix detected M-proteins in 41 of 58 Mass-Fix negative samples. This raised blood MRD positivity from 62 to 89 % against a BM NGF positivity rate of 51 %. Blood-BM agreement fell from 71 % (kappa 0.43) by Mass-Fix to 58 % (kappa 0.15) by HiRes Mass-Fix, driven by blood-positive/BM-negative discordance. IgG was overrepresented among discordant cases (68 vs. 45 %, p=0.003).HiRes Mass-Fix was successfully validated and demonstrated to increase M-protein detection in samples negative by Mass-Fix. IgG recycling may explain the blood-positive/BM-negative discordance, and serial measurements will be needed to distinguish residual M-protein from ongoing production. Blood-based M-protein measurement is a less invasive, lower-cost alternative to bone marrow biopsy for ongoing patient monitoring.© 2026 Walter de Gruyter GmbH, Berlin/Boston.

title: Metabolic gatekeepers shape immune cell function in rheumatoid arthritis.
abstract: Immune cell function is tightly coupled to cellular metabolism, with glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, and amino acid and lipid metabolism governing activation, differentiation, survival, and effector responses. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), an autoimmune disease characterized by destructive joint inflammation, metabolic checkpoints have emerged as critical regulators of immune-cell behavior and drivers of tissue pathology. RA CD4+ T cells undergo profound metabolic reprogramming: glycolysis is suppressed, and glucose is redirected into the pentose phosphate pathway, resulting in NADPH accumulation, reduced ROS levels, and a highly reductive intracellular environment. Concurrent defects in mitochondrial DNA repair and electron transport chain function compromise mitochondrial fitness, leading to NAD+ depletion, altered tricarboxylic acid cycle activity, and metabolic exhaustion. The resulting accumulation of citrate and acetyl-CoA promotes lipogenesis and protein acetylation, driving membrane remodeling, tissue invasiveness, and proinflammatory effector functions. Depletion of oxaloacetate and aspartate limits NAD+ regeneration, inducing endoplasmic reticulum expansion and enhanced tumor necrosis factor production. Defective lysosomal coordination of AMPK and mTORC1 signaling uncouples energy sensing from anabolic programs, enabling cellular activation and proliferation despite metabolic insufficiency. Macrophage fate and function are similarly shaped by metabolic state. In synovial macrophages, GLUD1-dependent glutamine oxidation sustains mitochondrial respiration and ATP production, enabling survival under nutrient-deprived conditions while promoting antigen presentation. Conversely, metabolic stress in MerTK+ macrophages activates the NAD+ hydrolase SARM1, triggering NAD+ depletion, mitochondrial collapse, and PANoptotic cell death. Together, these findings identify NAD+ availability, mitochondrial fitness, and organelle-based signaling as central metabolic gatekeepers linking bioenergetic stress to immune-cell dysfunction and chronic inflammation in RA.© 2026 The Author(s). title: From Evidence to Action: A Science-Driven Model for Training Cancer Advocates.
abstract: The Science of Community Outreach and Engagement (SoCOE) Cancer Advocacy Master Trainer Program is a theory-informed, community-engaged training model designed to advance cancer advocacy science and strengthen equitable cancer control infrastructure. Curriculum content was delivered using the Handbook for Cancer Advocacy (2nd edition, 2024), a 17-chapter structured curriculum developed by the Prostate Cancer Transatlantic Consortium and iCCaRE for Black Men Consortium. Grounded in the Social Ecological Model, Health Belief Model, Community-Based Participatory Research principles, implementation science, and cancer health equity frameworks, the program prepares advocates to function as knowledge brokers, dissemination agents, and implementation partners across individual, community, organizational, and policy levels. Forty advocates participated in the training; sixteen completed the post-training evaluation. Participants reported substantial increases in cancer-specific advocacy knowledge, confidence to train others, clinical trials literacy, and readiness for community-centered implementation. Qualitative findings indicated the emergence of a networked advocacy community characterized by peer learning and shared implementation strategies. These findings support science-based advocacy training as a scalable mechanism for integrating community voice into cancer care, research, and policy.© The Author(s) 2026. title: Association of GLP-1 receptor agonist use with mortality and healthcare utilization in patients with vascular dementia.
abstract: Patients with vascular dementia (VD) have high mortality and frequent acute care use, and no treatment has been shown to improve these outcomes. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are associated with a lower incidence of dementia and with cardiovascular benefit in type 2 diabetes, but their association with clinical outcomes in patients with established VD is unknown.This retrospective cohort study using a national database identified patients with VD from 2016 to 2025. Patients receiving GLP-1RAs within one month of diagnosis were propensity-score matched with non-users (n = 613 per group). Primary outcome was mortality at 1, 3, and 5 years; secondary outcomes included hospitalizations and emergency visits.GLP-1RA use was associated with lower risk of mortality at 1 year (8.7% vs. 15.9%; HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34-0.71), 3 years (23.3% vs. 33.8%; HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.44-0.76), and 5 years (34.4% vs. 54.3%; HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.41-0.69) (all p < 0.001). In addition, GLP-1RA use was associated with lower risk of inpatient admissions and emergency visits.GLP-1RA use in patients with VD was associated with lower risk of mortality and healthcare utilization. These beneficial associations warrant prospective randomized trials.© 2026. This is a U.S. Government work and not under copyright protection in the US; foreign copyright protection may apply.

title: Transient Cognitive Vulnerability After Hypoglycemia in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: Evidence From Continuous Glucose Monitoring and Cognitive Ecologic Momentary Assessment.
abstract: Adults with type 1 diabetes experience short-term changes in cognitive performance after glycemic events; however, the duration of such cognitive effects remains unclear. We examined whether hypoglycemic and hyperglycemic events and rapid glucose changes were associated with changes in processing speed or sustained attention in adults with type 1 diabetes and whether these associations varied by time since the event.Participants (N = 190) completed 15 days of smartphone-based ecologic momentary assessment (EMA; 3 prompts/day) paired with continuous glucose monitoring. Cognitive performance (median reaction time and accuracy) was tested using digit symbol matching (DSM) and gradual-onset continuous performance testing (GCPT; sustained attention) by TestMyBrain (processing speed). Glycemic exposures were defined as hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia lasting ≥15 min and rapid (5-min) increases or decreases in glucose >15 mg/dL, occurring during nonoverlapping intervals: 0-1, 1-2, and 2-3 h before EMA. Multilevel models estimated associations between glycemic exposures and cognitive performance, adjusting for age, EMA count, and interruptions.Hypoglycemic events occurring within 0-1 h of EMA were associated with slower reaction time and poorer performance on DSM and GCPT. No associations were observed for events occurring 1-2 or 2-3 h before EMA. Hyperglycemic events and rapid glucose increases or decreases were not associated with cognition across most outcomes or time windows.Hypoglycemia was associated with a transient period of cognitive vulnerability largely confined to the hour after an event, with little evidence of delayed effects. Findings support avoiding or exercising caution during cognitively demanding tasks for up to an hour after a hypoglycemic event.© 2026 by the American Diabetes Association.

title: A Crisis in the Treatment of Osteoporosis - 10 Years Later, the US Care Gap is Still Open.
abstract: A decade ago, we published an editorial in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research describing a crisis in osteoporosis treatment. In this Perspective, we reassess osteoporosis care and progress addressing that crisis. Despite the availability of safe and effective medications that reduce fracture risk, the osteoporosis care gap persists and may have widened in the United States (US). Fewer than 15% of patients receive osteoporosis therapy within one year of a fragility fracture, and treatment rates declined between 2015 and 2022. Meanwhile, declining hip fracture rates plateaued around 2012 and remain stable, while clinical vertebral fractures have increased. Persistent barriers include limited patient awareness of bone health, low screening rates, reduced access to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), concerns regarding treatment-related adverse events, underutilization of fracture liaison services, as well as racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic disparities. Despite this, the tools available to address the crisis have expanded. Advances that can help narrow the current care gap include new osteoanabolic agents; improved understanding of atypical femur fracture risk-benefit profiles; goal-directed treatment; opportunistic screening and diagnosis; artificial intelligence-enabled vertebral fracture detection; and electronic medical record-based decision support. Other developments may reduce the future burden of osteoporosis and fracture, including growing evidence supporting primary prevention, evolving perspectives on menopausal hormone therapy, and U.S. Food and Drug Administration qualification of total hip bone mineral density as a surrogate endpoint for fractures, which may facilitate more efficient drug development. The challenge now is to implement available approaches for patients at high fracture risk while continuing to consider strategies that shift osteoporosis care toward earlier prevention. title: The Modern Utility of Awake Deep Brain Stimulation Surgery.
abstract: Advances in neuroimaging and stereotactic accuracy have led many centers to adopt asleep workflows for deep brain stimulation (DBS), raising questions about the continued role of awake surgery with microelectrode recording. We evaluated whether intraoperative physiological testing during awake ventral intermediate nucleus (Vim) DBS results in trajectory adjustments that converge with the imaging-defined target.We retrospectively reviewed 137 consecutive Vim DBS leads implanted in awake patients. For each lead, we determined whether the final implant followed the planned trajectory, required a depth adjustment, or was moved to a parallel trajectory based on microelectrode recording and test stimulation. In cases involving parallel trajectory adjustments, coregistered preoperative imaging and postoperative computed tomography were used to compare the final lead position with the imaging-defined target and determine the direction and magnitude of deviation. Intraoperative ring stimulation data were analyzed to compare tremor suppression and side effects before and after trajectory adjustment.Of 137 leads, 116 (85%) were implanted along the planned trajectory, including 49 at the planned depth and 67 with depth adjustments. Twenty-one leads (15%) were moved to a parallel trajectory based on intraoperative findings; 17 had data suitable for spatial analysis. Among these, 13 (76%) were moved farther from the imaging-defined target, 2 (12%) an equal distance across the target, and 2 (12%) closer. In 12 cases with paired pre- and postadjustment stimulation testing, trajectory adjustment was associated with reduced stimulation required for near tremor resolution, increased side effect thresholds, and expansion of the therapeutic window. No leads required revision.Intraoperative physiological testing during awake Vim DBS frequently prompted trajectory adjustments that would not have been made under imaging guidance alone and were associated with improved stimulation response, underscoring the continuing role of awake testing in refining lead placement to patient-specific functional anatomy.Copyright © Congress of Neurological Surgeons 2026. title: Patient Report of Subsequent Uterine-Sparing Leiomyomata Procedures up to 10 Years.
abstract: To determine risk of subsequent treatment after uterine-sparing procedures for uterine leiomyomata.Study participants from two uterine leiomyomata procedure studies were recontacted. The baseline procedures studied included myomectomy, endometrial ablation, laparoscopic ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation (RFA), and uterine artery embolization (UAE). Participants reported all uterine leiomyomata procedures after their baseline uterine-sparing leiomyomata procedure. The subsequent treatment options analyzed included the baseline uterine leiomyomata procedures plus hysterectomy and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided focused ultrasonography. Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate differences in retreatment risk according to baseline procedure by means of hazard ratios (HRs) and corresponding 95% CIs. Fisher exact tests were used to examine the association between baseline procedure and retreatment procedure.The total number of participants in the study is 817. Median age at baseline procedure was 39.7 years; participant median age at recontact was 46.8 years. Follow-up after baseline procedure was 4.0-10.5 years. Baseline procedure types included myomectomy (n=469, 66.0%), endometrial ablation (n=90, 12.7%), RFA (n=96, 13.5%), and UAE (n=56, 7.9%). Of the 204 participants (28.7%) who had retreatment for uterine leiomyomata, the most common subsequent procedure was hysterectomy (n=94, 46.1%), followed by myomectomy (n=57, 27.9%), UAE (n=26, 12.7%), endometrial ablation (n=12, 5.9%), MRI-guided focused ultrasonography (n=9, 4.4%), and RFA (n=6, 2.9%). Within 5 years after the baseline procedure, 79.1% (95% CI, 76.2-82.1%) had no additional uterine procedures; 64.1% (95% CI, 57.7-71.2%) had none within 10 years. When endometrial ablation, RFA, and UAE were compared with myomectomy, RFA was found to have a higher retreatment rate (HR 1.61, 95% CI, 1.08-2.40). title: Phantom-Based Evaluation of a Novel Tomographic Ultra-Fast Molecular Breast Imaging Prototype.
abstract: A novel stationary tomographic Ultra-Fast Molecular Breast Imaging (UFMBI) technology was developed to reduce acquisition time and radiation dose of Molecular Breast Imaging (MBI), enabling its wider acceptance for supplemental dense breast screening. The system combines a stationary dual-head gamma camera made of CZT detectors with densely packed multi-pinhole collimators and novel de-multiplexing reconstruction methods, exploiting the ultra-high 3D position resolution of CZT detectors and their excellent energy resolution. A small field-of-view prototype (132 mm × 88 mm) was designed, built and calibrated. Raw detector data were processed using a machine-learning model providing 10×10 subpixelisation of 2 mm pixels in 5 mm thick CZT detectors and depth-of-interaction (DOI) estimation from anode signals alone. Tomographic images were reconstructed using an OSEM algorithm, including de-multiplexing and corrections for attenuation and collimator response. The prototype was evaluated using a 99mTc-filled phantom with lesions of different sizes and uniform background acquired separately. Prototype performance was compared with a clinical planar MBI system by imaging 99mTc-infused gel phantoms, with lesion detectability assessed via contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR). The results from the spheres' phantom indicated that 5-7 mm diameter lesions with tumour-to-background ratios of 10-20:1 were detectable even with a dose/time reduction factor (DRF) of 8 relative to current MBI clinical practice. The gel phantom experiments showed that, with equal activity concentration and scanning time (DRF=1), the UFMBI prototype provided 2.5 to 3.9-fold CNR of the clinical planar system depending on the lesion activity and position within the field-of-view; with DRF of 6, UFMBI provided 1.6 to 2.4-fold CNR of the clinical system, improving to 2.5 to 3.4-fold with application of non-local means noise filtering. These results suggest the technology could enable faster, safer breast cancer screening, though further development is needed before clinical use.

The prototype was assessed using 99mTc-filled phantoms with lesions of varying sizes, with tomographic images reconstructed via OSEM algorithm incorporating de-multiplexing and corrections for attenuation and collimator response, and lesion detectability measured by contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR). title: Prevalence and outcomes of co-occurring mental/physical comorbidities and substance use disorders: An atlas umbrella review including 156 systematic reviews with meta-analysis.
abstract: Substance use disorders(SUDs) are intertwined with psychiatric and general medical disorders. Substances of abuse also exert intrinsic toxicities and adverse effects that contribute to extensive somatic multimorbidity, complicating patient prognoses. This umbrella review(UR) systematically aggregated, harmonized, and graded the credibility of meta-analytic evidence concerning SUD comorbidities across psychiatric/somatic dimensions. We searched major electronic databases up to July 2026 for systematic reviews with meta-analyses of observational studies mapping SUD co-occurrences. Extracted data were categorized by ICD-11 diagnostic blocks. Meta-analytic estimates were evaluated using pre-registered quantitative credibility indicators assessing sample size(N), number of studies(k), 95%confidence interval(95%CI) widths, and heterogeneity(I2). The review included 156 systematic reviews with meta-analysis, encompassing 100,441,167 database/registry records across 14,322 study entries, with possible overlap across reviews. High-credibility data showed a strong intra-block psychiatric overlap: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder demonstrated a pooled SUD prevalence of 21.0%(95%CI=17.0-25.0%;k = 31), while Major Depressive Disorder reached a prevalence of 36.1%(95%CI=32.4%-39.7%;k = 161) among patients with Opioid Use Disorder(OUD). Somatic toxicities and iatrogenic pathways were highly prevalent: opioid analgesic use in chronic noncancer pain 27.0%(95%C.I.=23.0-31.0%;N > 3.9 M), and in post-lumbar fusion surgery patients (40.0%;95%C.I.=32.0-49.0%). High prevalences of syndemic infectious comorbidities were observed among populations with injection drug use, with Hepatitis C virus prevalence reaching 61.0%(95%CI=56.0-67.0%) in regional cohorts. Highly specific associations revealed that schizotypal traits strongly correlate with Cannabis Use Disorder(I2=0%). SUDs are multi-systemic disorders characterized by substantial cross-block psychiatric/medical multimorbidity. The breadth and the credibility gradient of multimorbidity argue for routine cross-domain screening and coordinated care, with model effectiveness left to trials.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. and ECNP. title: Distal Humerus Nonunion Following Failed Internal Fixation: How do the Outcomes of Internal Fixation and Total Elbow Arthroplasty Compare?
abstract: Distal humerus nonunions are difficult to treat. The supracondylar ostectomy and shortening (S.O.S.) technique, which combines humeral shortening, parallel plating, and bone grafting, maximizes the success of internal fixation. The purpose of this study was to compare the outcomes of the S.O.S. technique with the outcomes of total elbow arthroplasty (TEA) for distal humerus nonunions.This retrospective review identified 25 distal humerus nonunions treated with the S.O.S. procedure and 45 TEA's performed specifically for distal humerus nonunion at a single institution between 1995 and 2019. All elbows had undergone at least 1 prior fixation attempt. The S.O.S. cohort had a younger mean age and less common intra-articular nonunion compared to the TEA cohort. Sex, mean number of prior surgeries, history of open fracture, and history of infection were similar between groups. Outcomes included complications, reoperations, range of motion, and Mayo Elbow Performance Scores (MEPS).In the SOS cohort, 2 elbows were lost to follow-up, 21 elbows achieved union, and 2 elbows failed to heal and subsequently underwent conversion to a TEA. Complications occurred in 9 elbows (36%) following S.O.S. compared to 18 elbows (40%) following TEA (OR 0.8, p=0.7). The rates of all-cause reoperation were 48% (12 elbows) after S.O.S vs 27% (12) after TEA (OR 2.5, p=0.08). The S.O.S. cohort had a 100° mean flexion-extension arc compared to 115° for TEA (p=0.06) with similar mean pronation-supination arcs (S.O.S. 155° vs TEA 145°, p=0.2). MEPS scores were similar between groups (S.O.S 79 points, TEA 82 points, p=0.6). When stratifying by location of nonunion, elbows with intra-articular nonunion undergoing S.O.S had a 75% reoperation rate compared to 35% for extra-articular nonunions (OR 5.5, p=0.08). Intra-articular nonunions achieved higher MEPS with TEA compared to S.O.S. (85 vs. 51 points, p<0.01) while extra-articular nonunions achieved higher MEPS with S.O.S. compared to TEA (90 vs 65 points, p=0.01).Despite achieving a high union rate, the S.O.S. procedure presented similar results compared to TEA in terms of MEPS, motion, complications, and reoperations. Elbows with an intra-articular nonunion had better outcomes with TEA while elbows with an extra-articular nonunion fared better with the S.O.S.Copyright © 2026 American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons. title: Nutrition Care Strategies at the Intersection of Menopause and Obesity Pharmacotherapy.
abstract: The premenopause to menopause transition, known as perimenopause, is a critical period of metabolic vulnerability, characterized by hormonal changes, shifts in body composition, and increased cardiometabolic risk. Concurrently, incretin mimetic pharmacotherapies have emerged as highly effective treatments for obesity, achieving weight reductions that are approximating those previously observed only after bariatric surgery. While these agents confer substantial benefits, their mechanisms-appetite suppression, delayed gastric emptying, and enhanced satiety-introduce nutritional risks that intersect with pre-existing vulnerabilities of women experiencing this transition. Reduced energy intake and inadequate micronutrient intake, combined with estrogen deficiency, heighten the risk for osteoporosis and sarcopenic obesity. Likewise, gastrointestinal adverse events further compromise dietary quality and hydration, while aging physiology amplifies susceptibility to malnutrition. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on nutritional risks during perimenopause in the context of incretin mimetic pharmacotherapy, highlighting overlapping pathways that influence musculoskeletal health, metabolic resilience, and quality of life. Clinical strategies to mitigate these risks, including protein optimization, micronutrient monitoring, menopausal hormone therapy (osteoporosis/musculoskeletal health), and multidisciplinary care, are discussed alongside research priorities to inform targeted nutrition frameworks. Addressing these gaps is essential to ensure safe, effective, and sustainable obesity management for women in midlife and beyond.Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc.

llm_summary: This review examined how women going through menopause who take obesity medications face overlapping nutritional risks, including reduced food intake, inadequate vitamins and minerals, and weakened bones and muscles. The medications work by suppressing appetite and slowing digestion, which can help with weight loss but may compromise nutrition when combined with hormonal changes during menopause. The authors recommend strategies like increased protein intake, vitamin monitoring, and coordinated medical care to help women safely manage obesity during this life stage.
llm_summary_expert: This narrative review synthesizes evidence on nutritional risks for women transitioning through perimenopause who are receiving incretin mimetic pharmacotherapy for obesity management. The perimenopause transition creates metabolic vulnerability characterized by hormonal changes and altered body composition, while incretin mimetics produce weight reductions approximating bariatric surgery outcomes through appetite suppression, delayed gastric emptying, and enhanced satiety. The combination of reduced energy intake from these medications and estrogen deficiency during perimenopause heightens risk for osteoporosis and sarcopenic obesity, with gastrointestinal adverse events further compromising dietary quality and hydration status. Clinical strategies to mitigate these overlapping nutritional risks include protein optimization, micronutrient monitoring, menopausal hormone therapy for musculoskeletal health, and multidisciplinary care coordination. The review identifies critical research gaps and advocates for targeted nutrition frameworks to ensure safe and sustainable obesity management in midlife women experiencing this intersection of physiological transitions and pharmacological intervention.

title: Patient choice and uptake of Home-based rehabilitation with Health coaching versus Center-based pulmonary rehabilitation after a COPD-related hospitalization.
abstract: Adherence to center-based pulmonary rehabilitation after a COPD-related hospitalization-which improves all outcomes, including survival-is only 3%. Home-based programs have been proposed as a more feasible option, but they are not systematically offered, and patient preference is unknown.This pragmatic randomized trial involving patients with COPD recently hospitalized for a COPD exacerbation, originally aimed to investigate the comparative effect two arms: The choice of a facilitated referral to a center-based outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program or a home-based program versus a home-based program on adherence to post-hospitalization rehabilitation and disease-specific QoL measured by the Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire. The trial aimed to investigate the patient's preference of home vs center-based rehabilitation in individuals randomized to the choice arm. Daily steps were measured by Actigraph ®.The asynchronous home-based program included weekly health coaching and daily monitoring of daily steps, symptoms, and a 20-minute daily flexibility-balance exercise routine.Of 1,906 patients approached, 294 (15%) were randomized and agreed to the rehabilitation options offered by the study arms (uptake); of those, 56% completed the 12-week intervention (adherence). Of the 145 randomized to the choice arm, only one patient chose center-based PR; therefore, both groups received the same intervention, and results are presented as a one-group (before-after) analysis. Compared with baseline, the home intervention significantly improved (p < 0.01) physical and emotional QoL (Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire) and increased daily steps beyond the minimal clinically important difference. Trajectory models adjusted for age, FEV1%, and mMRC (breathlessness) confirmed sustained improvements in QoL at 6 and 12 months from baseline.When offered a choice of rehabilitation setting after a COPD-related hospital admission for an exacerbation, home-based rehabilitation is patients' preferred option. Sustained quality-of-life improvements in 1 year may represent an opportunity to regain well-being and/or deliver primary palliative care. Our results may have important implications for clinical practice.© The Author(s) 2026. Published by Oxford University Press on behalf of the American Thoracic Society.

title: Deciphering the molecular granularity of subependymomas and its distinction from posterior fossa ependymoma.
abstract: The CNS tumor classification of the WHO currently subsumes subependymomas (SE) of the supratentorial, infratentorial, and spinal compartment as one tumor type. Molecular data on SE are generally sparse, but SE are known to exhibit distinct global DNA methylation profiles according to their anatomical location. Previous studies indicate that a fraction of posterior fossa tumors exhibiting DNA methylation profiles of SE morphologically appear as ependymomas and may be prone to relapse.We assembled a cohort of ependymal tumors that best match supratentorial (n = 89), infratentorial (n = 146), or spinal (n = 45) SE DNA methylation profiles.Infratentorial tumors with an SE DNA methylation profile occurred at significantly higher ages with a male to female ratio of 4:1 and displayed two distinct subtypes. One of them (n = 49) was enriched for tumors that morphologically appear as ependymomas, carrying a loss of chromosome 6 as well as TERT promoter mutations. Respective patients showed a significantly shorter progression-free survival (p = 0.00014). Supratentorial SE frequently showed chromosome 8 loss while a small subset of tumors with a distinct DNA methylation profile and a segmentation of chromosome 6 was detected. Such chromosomal abnormalities were similarly observed in spinal SE.Based on clustering analysis and clinical features of tumors best matching a subependymoma methylation class, we postulate four subtypes of subependymomas. title: Scoping Review of Human Longitudinal Studies of Biomarkers Associated with Risk of Developing Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) to Inform the Development of a Novel SLE Risk Stratification Index.
abstract: SLE is often preceded by a preclinical phase in which autoantibodies and other biomarkers are detectable, offering an opportunity to identify at-risk individuals for early monitoring and testing interventions to halt progression. To inform an effort to develop SLE risk-stratification criteria, we conducted a scoping review of longitudinal human studies of biomarkers measured before SLE onset.Following PRISMA-ScR, we searched three databases and used a Population, Exposure, Comparator, Outcome framework to select longitudinal studies in which biomarkers were measured before an incident diagnosis or classification of SLE. Study characteristics, biomarkers, and outcomes were extracted from included studies.We included 59 original studies and two meta-analyses including heterogeneous at-risk populations, in which the proportion progressing to SLE varied widely. Most evidence concerned conventional serological markers, whereas interferon and cytokine signatures, proteomic panels, and genetic risk scores were examined in fewer, recent cohorts. Few biomarkers were studied across multiple populations or with comparable follow-up, outcome definitions, and analytic methods, and most associations came from single studies without external validation. Longitudinal biomarker trajectories before onset were rarely characterized, and non-European populations were under-represented.his review maps the breadth of candidate biomarkers associated with the risk of developing SLE and the heterogeneity of the evidence supporting them. Building a clinically useful SLE risk-stratification index will need a shared definition of the at-risk state, and prospective studies that follow biomarkers over time, in populations from broader geographical regions.This article is protected by copyright. title: From cross-reactivity to clinical utility: rethinking antigen testing for histoplasmosis and blastomycosis.
abstract: Circulating galactomannan antigen detection plays an important role in the diagnosis of histoplasmosis and blastomycosis. Historically, clinical laboratories have offered separate, genus-specific antigen detection assays across different specimen types for these two dimorphic pathogens. However, given their substantial geographic overlap, similar clinical presentation, comparable treatment approaches, and well-described antigenic cross-reactivity, the clinical rationale for maintaining separate, genus-specific antigen detection assays is increasingly unclear. In this Commentary, we propose that a combined, genus-agnostic Histoplasma/Blastomyces antigen detection assay represents a practical, evidence-aligned approach for diagnostic evaluation of these endemic mycoses.

title: Evaluation of a Nurse-Led Auricular Therapy Intervention for Palliative Care Patients.
abstract: Palliative care seeks to reduce symptom burden and stress for patients with serious illness, and complementary, nonpharmacologic approaches may improve comfort and patient empowerment. The authors retrospectively evaluated a nurse-led auricular acupressure program for patients with cancer receiving palliative care to assess its feasibility, tolerability, and symptom response. Palliative care registered nurses provided auricular acupressure to adult patients for cancer-associated symptoms in the inpatient and outpatient settings after completing specialized training, with didactic and hands-on components. The medical records of the first 200 patient visits for auricular acupressure from June 1, 2023, to February 28, 2024 were reviewed. The primary symptom of concern was identified, and symptom severity was recorded immediately before and after treatment using an 11-point Likert scale. Complete preintervention and postintervention data were available for 101 patients. Across symptoms, postintervention scores improved, with the most notable reductions observed for pain. Adverse effects were minimal. Patient comments described meaningful symptom relief, improved functioning, and decreased reliance on medications. Nurses reported that the workflow was feasible within routine practice and viewed the program as sustainable. Auricular acupressure appears to be a valuable, noninvasive adjunct for symptom management in palliative care. title: Assessment of Coronary Inflammatory Risk From Noncontrast Cardiac Computed Tomography.
abstract: Individuals with low or minimal coronary artery calcification (CAC) are considered at low cardiovascular risk, but a substantial absolute number of cardiovascular events occur in this population; assessment of coronary inflammation using the fat attenuation index (FAI) score may identify residual inflammatory risk beyond CAC score.To assess whether coronary inflammation measured on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) or noncontrast cardiac CT (NCCT) identifies individuals at high cardiovascular risk independent of CAC burden.In this cohort study, a novel artificial intelligence algorithm for measuring FAI score on NCCT was trained and tested in an independent, multicenter, longitudinal cohort of consecutive individuals undergoing clinically indicated CCTA and NCCT for CAC score between 2010 and 2021, with median (IQR) follow-up of 6.7 (4.6-10.0) years. Data were analyzed from January 2010 to March 2024.Agatston CAC score and coronary inflammation from both CCTA (CCTA FAI score, established biomarker) and NCCT (NC FAI score, novel biomarker).The primary outcome was cardiovascular (CV) mortality; the secondary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), comprising myocardial infarction, new-onset heart failure, or CV death.The derivation cohort included 6818 individuals (median [IQR] age, 61 [51-71] years; 3543 female participants [52.0%]), and the external validation clinical outcomes cohort included 19 110 individuals (median [IQR] age, 56.0 [48.0-64.0] years; 9289 female participants [48.6%]). During follow-up, 536 CV deaths and 1727 MACE occurred. FAI scores independently stratified CV mortality risk across CAC score categories, with the strongest associations among individuals with CAC score of 0. Adding CCTA FAI score or NC FAI score to CAC score significantly improved risk discrimination (area under the curve increased from 0.76 to 0.81 and 0.80, respectively; P < .001), reclassification (net reclassification index), and net benefit across all risk thresholds. Among 89 CV deaths in individuals with CAC score of 0 and 138 CV deaths with CAC score of 1 through 99, 44.9% and 44.2% had NC FAI score above the 75th percentile, respectively. Among individuals with CAC score of 0, CV mortality rates increased from 1.4 to 4.0 per 1000 person-years for those with NC FAI score above the 75th percentile, and MACE rates increased from 5.9 to 13.3 per 1000 person-years.Per the results of this cohort study, NC FAI score provides prognostic performance comparable to CCTA FAI score and improves cardiovascular risk prediction and reclassification beyond CAC score. Elevated FAI score, derived from either CCTA or NCCT, should be interpreted as a risk-enhancing factor that may prompt intensification of established, evidence-based preventive measures and may serve as a potential future gatekeeper for the use of targeted anti-inflammatory treatments.

title: Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma genomic profiling demonstrates thymic B-cell identity and frequent aberrant somatic hypermutation.
abstract: Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) is a subtype of non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that most frequently occurs in young adults and is thought to reflect neoplastic transformation of thymic medullary B-cells. We characterized 59 PMBL cases from the Atlas of Blood Cancer Genomes Project. The cohort was predominantly young (median age 35), female (62%), and included individuals from diverse racial backgrounds. Most individuals presented with low-stage disease, favorable ECOG performance status, and high overall survival rate at last follow-up (89%). Whole transcriptome sequencing of 49 PMBL cases revealed gene expression profiles distinct from diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (DLBCL, NOS), both activated B cell-like (ABC) and germinal center B cell-like (GCB) cell-of-origin subtypes. PMBLs showed significantly higher expression of thymic B cell-associated genes (p=0.032), supporting their presumed thymic origin. Whole exome and targeted sequencing confirmed recurrent mutations in JAK/STAT, NF-κB signaling, and DNA damage response pathways, with frequent aberrant somatic hypermutation (aSHM) affecting multiple genes. Recurrent copy number alterations included gains at 9p and 12, and losses at 13q. As in prior studies, CIITA rearrangements with diverse partners were recurrent. Although PMBL generally demonstrates excellent outcomes, aSHM-positive cases exhibited inferior progression-free survival (p=0.031), suggesting aSHM as a potential adverse prognostic marker. Our findings further refine the genomic landscape of PMBL and provide new insights into the biology of this neoplasm, with implications for prognostic stratification.

llm_summary: Researchers studied 59 cases of primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma, a blood cancer affecting young adults, to understand its genetic characteristics and origins. They found that this cancer arises from thymic B-cells and identified frequent genetic mutations in specific cell signaling pathways, along with a pattern of aberrant genetic changes that was associated with worse progression-free survival. These findings suggest that testing for this aberrant genetic pattern could help identify patients who need more aggressive treatment.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers characterized 59 primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) cases from the Atlas of Blood Cancer Genomes Project, predominantly comprising young adults (median age 35) with 62% female representation and diverse racial backgrounds. Whole transcriptome sequencing of 49 cases and whole exome sequencing revealed gene expression profiles distinct from diffuse large B-cell lymphoma subtypes, with significantly higher expression of thymic B cell-associated genes (p=0.032) supporting thymic origin. Recurrent mutations were identified in JAK/STAT, NF-κB signaling, and DNA damage response pathways, with frequent aberrant somatic hypermutation affecting multiple genes and recurrent copy number alterations including gains at 9p and 12 and losses at 13q. Cases with aberrant somatic hypermutation exhibited inferior progression-free survival (p=0.031) compared to those without this feature, suggesting it as a potential adverse prognostic marker. Most individuals presented with low-stage disease and favorable performance status, achieving an 89% overall survival rate at last follow-up, though the prognostic significance.

title: Modernization of a Historical Prostate Cancer Registry using Artificial Intelligence: A Tale of Two Large Language Models.
abstract: Since 1986, the Mayo Clinic Prostate Cancer Registry has followed over 30,000 patients who underwent radical prostatectomy. Advances in LLMs may modernize data collection, reduce human abstraction burden, and improve registry efficiency. Herein, we report the results of LLM data abstraction for surgical pathology and prostate MRI data in the Mayo Clinic Prostate Cancer Registry.Surgical pathology and MRI reports were obtained for 3,210 and 4,739 patients, respectively, who underwent radical prostatectomy from 2010-2022. LLM prompts for 13 pathology and 20 MRI variables were developed and ran through two independent LLMs (Google Gemini Flash 1.5, 2.0, or 2.5). LLM outputs were compared to human-abstracted data.Median consensus LLM error rate for pathology report data was 0.09%(IQR 0.03-0.16%), compared with median human error rate of 2.81%(IQR 1.83-3.17%). Individual LLMs had threefold higher error rates compared to consensus LLM (LLM 1: 0.27%(IQR 0.09-0.34%), LLM 2: 0.30%(IQR 0.17%-0.48%)). For MRI reports, median consensus LLM error rate was 0.17%(IQR 0.00-0.68%), compared with human error rate of 1.01%(IQR 0.59-3.20%). Individual LLMs had error rates of 0.84%(IQR 0.34-2.79%) and 1.02%(IQR 0.34-1.67%). Estimated time for human data abstraction across all 136,510 data elements was 952 hours, compared with 32 hours for our LLM pipeline.LLM data abstraction employing a consensus vote across two independent LLMs consistently yielded higher accuracy than human or single-LLM abstraction. A dual-LLM consensus architecture may improve data abstraction efficiency, reduce errors, and should be considered for integration into all prospectively maintained longitudinal clinical registries.

title: Potential Impact of Breathing Practice on Brain and Mental Health in Rural Adolescents With Psychiatric Symptoms: Protocol for a Single-Arm Pilot Feasibility Trial.
abstract: Mental health conditions (MHC), particularly depression and anxiety, are the leading contributors to youth disability globally. In the United States, there has been a steep increase in diagnosed MHC cases over the last decade. Adolescents in rural areas are disproportionately affected by the combination of limited access to mental health professionals and stigma around seeking care. Current treatment options, mainly psychotherapy and psychopharmacology, have shown modest effects. Prior research suggests associations between slow-paced deep breathing and autonomic function, cerebral perfusion, and stress regulation, supporting further investigation of structured breathing as a potential adjunctive approach for MHC management.This study aims to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, implementation appropriateness, and participant satisfaction of a digitally supported, breathing-based intervention for adolescents with mild-to-moderate anxiety and depressive symptoms. The study will assess recruitment, retention, intervention engagement, usability, and the feasibility of collecting physiological and patient-reported outcome data to inform the design of a future efficacy trial.We aim to recruit approximately 40 adolescent patients receiving care through the Mayo Clinic Health System from rural communities in northwestern Wisconsin and southeastern Minnesota. Participants will complete a 4-month structured breathing program delivered entirely online, supported by a mobile app for guided instruction and practice tracking. All participants will attend 2 in-person visits (baseline and 4 mo) for functional near-infrared spectroscopy, as participants will already be on-site, the baseline and final study assessments will be completed at these same visits. A subsample (n=10) will additionally undergo magnetic resonance imaging at these visits.This study was funded in October 2025, and data collection began in February 2026, with completion anticipated in late 2026. As of July 2026, 14 of the 40 (35%) planned participants have been enrolled. Analysis will follow completion of data collection, with results expected to be reported in early 2027.Adolescents with anxiety and depression are a particularly vulnerable group, often undertreated due to limited access to mental health care. The proposed breathing intervention is designed as an accessible and scalable approach that warrants feasibility evaluation in rural youth populations.© Pravesh Sharma, Kaylynn Imsande, Danielle Boos, Nicholas L Bormann, Rowa Osman, Marin Nycklemoe, Seokbeen Lim, Stephan Arndt, Jana Kainerstorfer, Paul H Min. llm_summary: Researchers are testing whether a smartphone app that guides breathing exercises could help rural teenagers with anxiety and depression, a group often unable to access mental health care. The study involves 40 adolescents completing a four-month online breathing program with in-person brain imaging visits, and as of mid-2026, about one-third of participants had enrolled. Results from this feasibility study, expected in early 2027, will determine whether breathing exercises are practical and acceptable enough to test more rigorously in future research.

Participants complete a 4-month structured breathing program with assessments at baseline and 4 months including functional near-infrared spectroscopy at both in-person visits, while a subsample of 10 participants additionally undergoes magnetic resonance imaging to evaluate cerebral perfusion and brain activity. As of July 2026, 14 of 40 planned participants (35%) have been enrolled, with data collection ongoing and completion anticipated in late 2026. title: The interaction between polygenic risk scores for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder is associated in healthy subjects with resting-state prefrontal activity linked with depressive symptoms in patients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.
abstract: Mood symptoms often characterize schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD). However, their biological underpinnings remain poorly defined. Given that these symptoms are a core feature of bipolar disorders (BD), and that BD-related genetic liability is also present in schizophrenia (SCZ), genetic variation for each disorder may jointly interact to modulate brain phenotypes relevant for mood symptoms in SSD.To test this interaction, we computed Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) for SCZ and BD in 263 healthy participants (HP) using diagnosis-associated variants at the genome-wide level significance (PRS_SCZ_GWA, PRS_BD_GWA) or at p < 0.05 (PRS_SCZ_05, PRS_BD_05) with the clumping and thresholding method. We also calculated further PRSs using the Bayesian continuous shrinkage method (PRS_CS_SCZ, PRS_CS_BD) to verify our results using a different approach. Spontaneous brain activity was estimated using the fractional Amplitude of Low Frequency Fluctuations (fALFF). Finally, the relationship between fALFF and mood symptoms was investigated on an independent sample of 40 SSD.In HP, multiple regression indicated a PRS_SCZ_05 by PRS_BD_05 interaction on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and angular gyrus (AG) fALFF, such that lower PRS_SCZ_05 and higher PRS_BD_05 was associated with lower DLPFC fALFF, whereas higher scores of both PRSs were associated with greater AG fALFF. PRS_CS analysis yielded convergent results in left DLPFC. In SSD, DLPFC fALFF negatively correlated with depressive symptoms.These findings suggest that genetic risk for SCZ and BD jointly modulates spontaneous brain activity in HP in areas that may be relevant to depressive symptoms in SSD. Clinical heterogeneity of SCZ may thus reflect the cross-talk between SCZ- and BD-related genetic pathways.Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier B.V.
