title: Cutaneous Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma: A Single-Center Retrospective Clinical, Histopathologic, and Molecular Review of 13 Cases of Primary Cutaneous ALCL and Cutaneous Involvement of Systemic ALCL in Adults.
abstract: Anaplastic large cell lymphomas (ALCLs) are a heterogeneous group of CD30-positive mature T-cell lymphomas that share clinical and histopathologic characteristics but are distinct in clinical course, treatment recommendations, and outcomes.A single-center retrospective review of clinical, histopathologic, and molecular data of adult patients with cutaneous ALCL, for whom clinical features and biopsy tissue were available for review, was performed.Thirteen patients were included: 9 with primary cutaneous ALCL (pcALCL) and 4 with cutaneous involvement of systemic ALCL (3 anaplastic lymphoma kinase-negative systemic ALCL, 1 anaplastic lymphoma kinase-positive systemic ALCL). Ulcerated tumors (69%) and/or nodules (85%) involving the trunk (62%) and lower extremities (54%) were the most common clinical presentation for both groups. Patients with cutaneous involvement of systemic ALCL presented more commonly with clusters of 10 or greater tumors, lymphadenopathy (P = 0.007) and had poor outcomes, including death during the follow-up period (P = 0.014). Histopathologically, patients with systemic ALCL were more likely to have large pleomorphic multinucleated cells within the atypical infiltrate (P = 0.077). Other assessed clinical findings, histopathologic features, and molecular aberrations (including DUSP22 rearrangements), were identified in similar proportions between pcALCL and systemic ALCL.This study confirms that histopathologic, immunophenotypic and molecular features of pcALCL and cutaneous involvement of systemic ALCL demonstrate considerable overlap. This series highlights the necessity of correlation with clinical findings and ancillary studies before rendering a definitive diagnosis.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). title: Revised Reference Intervals for Serum Free Light Chains: Implementation at the Mayo Clinic.
abstract: Universal reference intervals (RIs) for serum free light chains (FLCs) were established in 2002 using nephelometric instrumentation and early-generation reagents. Since then, assay platforms have evolved, renal effects have been characterized, and lot-to-lot drift has been documented. Large population-based studies also proposed age- and kidney function-stratified RIs. We evaluated whether legacy RIs remain appropriate following transition to a turbidimetric platform with stabilized reagents and established updated RIs.Serum samples from 489 screened healthy adults were analyzed using the Optilite assay with stabilized κ calibrators. Samples with monoclonal proteins assayed by MASS-FIX, mass spectrometry-based monoclonal protein detection assay, were excluded. Central 99% RIs were derived using nonparametric methods. A secondary cohort of 106 individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) was analyzed to evaluate the effect of renal function. To assess clinical impact, 2025 clinical results, including >20 000 MASS-FIX-negative samples, were reclassified using legacy and revised RIs.The 2002 RIs were not verified in this contemporary cohort with 24.9% and 5.3% exceeding the historical upper limits for κFLC and κ/λ ratio, respectively. Newly established 99% RIs are 0.61 to 4.02 mg/dL for κ, 0.67 to 3.46 mg/dL for λ, and 0.57 to 2.45 for the κ/λ ratio. Lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was associated with increased FLC concentrations but smaller effects on the κ/λ ratio. Among MASS-FIX negative clinical samples, revised RIs reduced abnormal high flagging for κ/λ ratio from 17.6% to 4.1%.Legacy FLC RIs do not verify due to assay updates. Nonparametric 99% RIs better reflect contemporary assay performance and substantially reduce clinically meaningful misclassification.© The Author(s) 2026. title: Risk of Cancer in Autoimmune Pancreatitis: A Comparative Cohort Analysis Using SEER Population-Based Data.
abstract: Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) is a chronic fibroinflammatory pancreatic disease classified as Type 1, Type 2, and not otherwise specified (AIP-NOS). Although chronic pancreatitis is associated with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), malignancy risk in AIP remains uncertain. We aimed to assess incidence of PDAC and extrapancreatic cancers in AIP and compare with population estimates.We conducted a comparative cohort study of adults diagnosed with AIP by International Consensus Diagnostic Criteria between 2000-2023, excluding patients with prior or concurrent PDAC. Cancer outcomes were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards models and incidence rates per 1000 person-years, adjusting for age, sex, and relapse. Expected cancer incidence was derived from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database and compared using Poisson regression to estimate risk ratios (RRs).Among 282 patients with AIP (199 Type 1, 64 Type 2, 19 AIP-NOS), patients with Type 1 AIP were older, predominantly male, had higher smoking rates, and more frequent relapses (all p<0.05). Cancer incidence was highest in Type 1 AIP (23.7 per 1000 person-years; 95% CI 16.4-33.1; p=0.045). Relapses did not increase cancer risk. Compared to age- and sex-adjusted SEER estimates, overall cancer risk in AIP was not increased (RR 1.30; 95% CI 0.95-1.78; p=0.10). However, PDAC risk was significantly higher (RR 3.67; 95% CI 1.18-11.38; p=0.024), primarily in Type 1 AIP (RR 4.24; 95% CI 1.37-13.13; p=0.012).Type 1 AIP was associated with the highest observed incidence of pancreatic and extrapancreatic malignancies in this cohort. title: Randomized Phase II Clinical Trials in Rare Cancer Populations.
abstract: Single-arm phase II trials are commonly used in rare cancers because randomized trials are considered infeasible. However, single-arm designs depend on historical control benchmarks that may be uncertain or misspecified. We evaluated the operating characteristics of single-arm and small randomized designs for binary efficacy end points in rare cancer settings. Simulation studies were conducted for trials with sample sizes up to 100 patients. Single-arm trial outcomes were compared with a historical control. Simulations examined the impact of uncertainty and systematic misspecification in the historical control estimate. Randomized designs were compared with single-arm designs using the same total sample size and decision rules requiring the experimental arm to exceed the control arm by more than a prespecified number of successes. A sarcoma trial evaluating regorafenib plus nivolumab was used as an illustrative example. Single-arm trials were well calibrated when the historical control value was fixed and correctly specified. Uncertainty in the historical control value and systematic underestimation increased the probability of declaring a regimen promising despite no treatment benefit. In contrast, small randomized designs were largely insensitive to historical-control misspecification. In the sarcoma example, the planned single-arm design had favorable operating characteristics when the historical 4-month progression-free survival rate was assumed correct and precise. Uncertainty or misspecification of this estimate materially altered those characteristics. For rare cancers, single-arm phase II trials can be efficient when historical control rates are accurate and precise, but their conclusions are fragile when benchmarks are uncertain or biased. Small randomized phase II designs provide internally controlled screening evidence and should be considered when historical control values are uncertain.

title: Multimodal profiling identifies an HLH-spectrum inflammatory program in OHI-positive lymphoma patients.
abstract: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) in patients with hematologic malignancies (HM) is increasingly recognized but poorly understood. The Optimized HLH/HyperInflammation (OHI) index, based on HLH-related inflammatory markers (soluble CD25 and ferritin), identifies HM patients with very poor outcomes. However, the similarity of this malignancy-related inflammatory process to familial HLH (F-HLH) is unknown and the mechanisms underlying OHI+ hyperinflammation remain undefined. We profiled 7,288 serum proteins in OHI- and OHI+ lymphoma patients, F-HLH patients, and pediatric controls. OHI+ proteomes displayed clear evidence of widespread immune activation, compared to OHI- ones, characterized by T-cell, macrophage, multi-cytokine (including interferon-γ, IL-6, and IL-2) and complement activation. Unsupervised clustering revealed similarity between OHI+ lymphoma and F-HLH proteomes, with more than half of the differentially expressed proteins overlapping, highly concordant fold changes (R=0.96), and a shared inflammatory program. In an independent cohort of patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays confirmed increased expression of representative proteins from OHI+-enriched pathways. Flow cytometry demonstrated an increase in recently activated CD8+ T cells (CD38high/HLA-DR+) in OHI⁺ patients. Finally, we observed an increase in CD8+ T cells and CD68+ macrophages in OHI+ diagnostic lymph node biopsies. Thus, OHI positivity identified coordinated systemic and tissue-level immune activation which has notable similarity to F-HLH, suggesting that the OHI identifies an HLH-like spectrum of harmful inflammation in patients with newly diagnosed lymphomas. These findings provide a biologic validation for clinical OHI Index classification of lymphoid malignancies and support evaluation of targeted immunomodulation as a rational therapeutic strategy.Copyright © 2026 American Society of Hematology.

title: Childhood maltreatment and epigenetic age acceleration in adulthood: Moderation by obesity risk.
abstract: Childhood maltreatment is associated with elevated morbidity and mortality, potentially through accelerated epigenetic aging. Whether this association varies by adult body mass index (BMI) remains unclear.This 20-year prospective longitudinal study examined the main and interactive effects of childhood maltreatment and adult BMI on epigenetic aging.Participants were drawn from a cohort with documented childhood maltreatment and socioeconomically matched non-maltreated children. The adult sample included 368 participants (mean age = 30.92 years; 51% female; 57.3% Black, 25.3% White, and 5.1% multiracial); blood-derived DNA methylation data were available for 173. Participants with BMI data were predominantly overweight or had obesity.Childhood maltreatment (experiences occurring through age 12) was assessed using coded Child Protective Services records supplemented by adult retrospective reports. Epigenetic aging was indexed using Horvath, PhenoAge, DunedinPACE, GrimAge 1, and GrimAge 2. Regression models tested maltreatment, BMI, and their interaction, adjusting for covariates.Higher adult BMI was associated with accelerated epigenetic aging across multiple clocks. Significant maltreatment-by-BMI interactions emerged using the composite maltreatment measure for GrimAge 1 (β = -0.27) and GrimAge 2 (β = -0.36). Childhood maltreatment was associated with greater age acceleration among individuals with lower BMI, whereas those with higher BMI showed accelerated aging regardless of maltreatment history.Childhood maltreatment may have long-term implications for epigenetic aging, with associations varying by adult BMI. Findings highlight the value of examining how early adversity and adult metabolic risk jointly shape biological aging.Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

abstract: Evidence supporting steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (SSIs) in fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (f-HP) remains limited.Do SSIs improve lung function or survival in adults with f-HP?Following Cochrane and PRISMA 2020 guidance (PROSPERO CRD420261413825), we searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar through May 2026 for studies of mycophenolate, azathioprine, methotrexate, leflunomide, tacrolimus, or cyclophosphamide. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted, and appraised studies using ROBINS-I, JBI, or Newcastle-Ottawa tools. DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models pooled percent-predicted FVC and DLCO changes and hazard ratios for death or lung transplantation. GRADE assessed certainty.Seventeen studies (1,341 patients) were included. SSIs were associated with modest FVC stabilization (13 studies; +1.11% predicted, 95% CI 0.37-1.84; I2=0%) and DLCO stabilization (9 studies; +3.73% predicted, 95% CI 2.56-4.90; I2=24%). The estimand-consistent mortality pool of two adjusted overall-effect studies demonstrated no survival benefit and could not exclude harm (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.86-2.26; I2=0%). llm_summary: Researchers examined whether steroid-sparing immunosuppressants—drugs that reduce the need for steroids—could improve lung function or survival in adults with fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, a serious lung disease. The analysis of 17 studies found these medications produced only modest stabilization of lung function with no clear survival benefit. The evidence remains too limited to recommend these treatments, and researchers call for larger, well-designed trials to determine their true effectiveness.
llm_summary_expert: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies involving 1,341 patients examined whether steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (mycophenolate, azathioprine, methotrexate, leflunomide, tacrolimus, or cyclophosphamide) improve lung function or survival in adults with fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis. The primary endpoints were percent-predicted forced vital capacity (FVC) and diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) changes, along with hazard ratios for death or lung transplantation, analyzed using random-effects meta-regression models with GRADE certainty assessment. Steroid-sparing immunosuppressants were associated with modest FVC stabilization (+1.11% predicted) and DLCO stabilization (+3.73% predicted), while the mortality analysis of two adjusted studies showed no survival benefit and could not exclude harm (hazard ratio 1.39, 95% confidence interval 0.86–2.26). The certainty of evidence was rated as low for lung function outcomes and very low for mortality, with modest lung-function stabilization.

title: Artificial intelligence literacy among health-care professionals: a systematic review of reported competency needs.
abstract: Widespread calls for artificial intelligence (AI) literacy among health-care professionals have outpaced evidence on the AI information that should be taught and prioritised. We conducted a systematic review of studies published until Feb 12, 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (protocol preregistered on Open Science Framework). 70 studies comprising 42 empirical and 28 perspective or commentary papers from 21 countries were included after screening 4095 records. Among empirical studies, conceptual understanding of the meaning of AI (AI fundamentals; 88·1%), application of ethical thinking to AI use in clinical practice (ethical reasoning; 71·4%), and knowledge of existing AI tools (tools and applications; 71·4%) were the most prevalent competency domains. Perspective papers showed a similar pattern, with comparatively less emphasis on tools and applications. In 20 studies that asked students and health-care professionals to rank competencies by importance, tools and applications and the ability to evaluate AI before adoption (pre-adoption evaluation) ranked the highest. llm_summary: Researchers reviewed 70 studies to identify what artificial intelligence knowledge healthcare professionals should learn, finding that understanding AI basics, thinking through ethical concerns, and knowing about existing AI tools were the most commonly emphasized competencies. When students and professionals ranked these skills by importance, they prioritized learning to evaluate AI tools before using them in clinical practice. These findings provide a foundation for developing standardized AI training programs for healthcare workers.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers conducted a systematic review of 70 studies (42 empirical and 28 perspective or commentary papers) from 21 countries published through February 2026 to identify artificial intelligence literacy competencies that health-care professionals should prioritize. Among the empirical studies, conceptual understanding of AI fundamentals was the most prevalent competency domain at 88.1%, followed by ethical reasoning in clinical AI use at 71.4% and knowledge of existing AI tools and applications at 71.4%. When students and health-care professionals ranked competencies by importance in 20 studies, tools and applications and pre-adoption evaluation ability ranked highest, whereas perspective papers showed comparatively less emphasis on tools and applications. The findings reveal a discrepancy between the competency domains most frequently addressed in empirical research and those ranked as most important by learners and practitioners. These results provide a foundation for developing clinical AI competency frameworks, though the review does not establish which competencies most effectively improve clinical outcomes or professional practice.
